Subscribers were what mattered, because most of the views came from the sub feed. And videos went viral usually by getting a lot of attention elsewhere, like on Reddit or Facebook, not due to the YouTube algorithm. But once you had a big video and people subscribed, well, then your next video would likely get a lot of views from those subscribers. So YouTube would take that popular video and share it with more people. And so you'd get more subscribers in a positive feedback loop. But soon, YouTube realized that this did not create the best experience for the viewer. They discovered that showing people only videos from channels they were subscribed to led to fewer clicks, less watch time and less engagement with the site as a whole. Plus, they knew that relying on other platforms to drive traffic to viral hits was risky, since those other platforms might disable the traffic at any time. So they needed to make YouTube a destination in itself. They wanted people to come to YouTube, see videos that interested them, click on at least one of them and watch it for a while. Ideally get sucked down the YouTube rabbit hole and spend hours on the site without even noticing it. The ultimate resource is people's time and attention, and every platform is trying to capture as much of it as possible. So, to make YouTube this go-to destination, they had decrease the importance of subscribers, make it less like a podcast app where you only get the shows you're subscribed to, and more like Reddit, where stuff with the most engagement rises to the top. But that necessarily meant increasing the importance of clickbait. Now, there seems to be a paradox when it comes to clickbait. People almost universally claim to hate it, but you also see it everywhere. So why is this? Well, one of the problems is we don't all agree on the definition of clickbait. When I google it, the top definition is, on the internet, content whose main purpose is to attract attention and encourage visitors to click on a link to a particular webpage. We could call this type I clickbait, and there doesn't seem to be anything wrong with it. I mean, if you didn't try to attract attention and get people to click on your links, then you wouldn't really be doing your job. But there is a second definition. One that I think more people ascribe to, which is something such as a headline designed to make readers want to click on a hyperlink, especially when the link leads to content of dubious value or interest. Wikipedia says, "A defining characteristic of clickbait is that it is sensationalized or misleading." And it also talks about teasers that intentionally withhold information to exploit the "curiosity gap." They give you enough information to make you curious, but not enough to satisfy that curiosity. Here are two actual titles from a news website. Nine out of 10 Americans are completely wrong about this mind blowing fact. And someone gave some kids some scissors. Here's what happened next. I think we can all agree that these are examples of bad type II clickbait. Now, imagine a clickbait space where on one axis, you have how misleading or sensationalized it is. And on the other, how much information is intentionally withheld to create a curiosity gap. Well, then these two titles fall in the top right corner. And these are the zones of type II clickbait. At the other extreme, you have things that are so unsensationalized as to be dull. You could call this the dead zone. Now, here is where you would find "Strange applications of the Magnus Effect." I mean, I didn't tell you what the applications were. Now, in the middle is where you would find type I clickbait. But honestly, I think type I and type II clickbait are so different, that we shouldn't even use the same word for them. Instead of type I clickbait, my friend and YouTuber, Brady Heron suggested legitbait. I mean, it might sound enticing, but it is legit. Instead of type II clickbait, we could use clicktrap, clicktrick, linktrap or dupechute. What's important to recognize is that for any given video, there is no one true title and thumbnail. Each video could have hundreds or thousands of different legitbait titles. For example, how does a zero-G plane work? I went on a plane that does parabolic trajectories. What happens to fire on a zero-G plane? Now, the most enticing titles and thumbnails are found close to type II clickbait. I'm reminded of the infographic by smarter every day, showing that on social media, the greatest engagement occurs close to the boundary of what's allowable. But remember that everyone's definition of clickbait is different, and everyone's perceptions of words and images are different. So these are not clear boundaries. They're actually kind of fuzzy. What for one person might be legitbait, for someone else, could be a clicktrap. What's clear is that on a site where click-through rate is important, clickbait of all types is inevitable. How important to a video's success is the title and thumbnail? - Very important. Of course. If they don't click on the video, they don't watch it. If you don't begrudge the giraffe its long neck so it can reach the highest leaves, can you begrudge a YouTuber the red arrow that allows them to reach further audiences? I talked about this in my video two years ago. To be successful as a YouTuber, you need to optimize two things, watch time and the click-through rate of your videos. That's the number of times the title and thumbnail are clicked, divided by the total number of times they're shown. That's the number of impressions. Now at the time, this was something of a revelation for me because I always thought my job was to make great videos. And then a title and thumbnail that adequately represented what the video was about. But now I've realized that making the title and thumbnail is at least half the job. This is not just because better titles and thumbnails get you more clicks, but because better titles and thumbnails will get you way more impressions. YouTube has limited real estate with which to show you virtually infinite content. And so it's not enough to make a good video even if people watch all of it, you also have to make a title and thumbnail that gets clicked, especially in competition with other really good titles and thumbnails. That's the only way you can expect YouTube to give you more impressions. Now, the big development since my last video on this is YouTube introduced real-time metrics like views, impressions and click-through rate. Now, I suggested this would create an arms race. So what you can bet will happen is that creators will launch a video and then they'll be sitting there with all these different variants of thumbnails and they'll be swapping them out and looking at what that does to click-through rate and then going with the one that leads to the greatest click-through rate. And this is basically what has happened. Let me give you my favorite example. Last year, I made a video about asteroids, which I thought was really good. I called it "Asteroids: Earth's Biggest Threat," which is something Stephen Hawking said. And people were very positive about the video. And immediately the video started doing better. It quickly shot up from almost my worst performing video to my best. It now has 14 million views. Nothing about the video changed, just that one image and 38 characters. But because of that, the video has reached nearly 10 times as many people as it otherwise would have. And the title and thumbnail accurately describe what the video is about. I mean, sure, there's a curiosity gap, but you couldn't explain the whole concept in the length of the title. So if you see a YouTuber changing titles and thumbnails, this is why. Because that effort can be rewarded many times over. I've seen people objecting to this practice because they think the creator is trying to dupe their audience, get them to click on the same video more than once, but that's not it. The whole point is to get YouTube to show the title and thumbnail to more people. We're trying to increase the number of impressions, which is heavily dependent on the click-through rate. And this makes the viewer hold on longer for the hook. Now, the second way to solve for the relevance problem is to frame your hooks around expected value. There are two types of videos: entertainment and education. Both of these offer solutions to a painoint. That solution is value. Entertainment offers a solve for boredom. Education offers a solve for a specific problem. If you want your hook to feel more relevant for your viewer, all you have to do is agitate a painoint that they already have so that you can tee up a solution that is for them. For example, can you tell the difference between these two hooks? The first one is these are three common trends in skincare. And the second one is if you struggle with acne, try these three things. Learning about trends in skincare is a nice to have. Solving my acne problem is a need to have. So, if you frame the hook around a known painoint and you deliver it using you and your instead of me and my, the video will seem more targeted for the viewer and it will hook them more. Okay, the last hook problem number four is disinterest. And this is the one that most people fixate on the most. At this point, the viewer is clear on the topic, believes there is some relevance or value incoming for them, but the hook still just doesn't grab them enough. This is the curiosity problem. The hook just doesn't make the viewer curious enough to want to keep watching. So, what you want to do in the hook to solve the disinterest problem is build a curiosity loop. And everybody talks about curiosity loop, but nobody ever explains what it is. A curiosity loop is when the viewer sees something, asks a hypothetical question in their mind, gets some additional context to answer it, but that spurs a new question, more context, new question, more context, and so on. They keep opening loops throughout the entire video. That's what a curiosity loop really is. So, your job in the hook is to open that initial curiosity loop and start the spiral. What is that initial question that the viewer has where they can't look away? They just have to wait for more context to answer it. So, the $10 million content question really is this. How do you always drive curiosity and build that curiosity loop every single time, no matter what type of video you're making? And the way you do this is by setting up contrast or comparison in the hook. Contrast is simply the distance between the current common belief of the viewer and some contrarian or alternative perspective that you offer. So, for example, if I say in the hook, this one trick will clear up all your acne in 45 minutes without any side effects. What I'm really doing is creating a comparison in your mind to the current baseline. You got to wait 6 months, take Accutane, go through all these side effects versus my contrarian offer, 45 minutes, no side effects, quick solve. That distance is contrast. What happens when you do this in the viewer subconscious is that when you frame a comparison, A something they know and B something they don't, B triggers the sticky pain point they have from A not solving their pain. And so essentially that comparison acts as a reagitator of that painoint which gets them curious because they want to solve it. To simplify all this, if you're not following what I'm saying, it's A versus B. A is what they already believe. B is some alternative that you're suggesting that makes their pain point solved faster, better, or cheaper. Now, getting good at learning how to create this contrast with words is really the secret to driving curiosity whenever you want. It's honestly the secret to storytelling at a macro level. Now, I'm not going to go too deep into exactly how to build this contrast and curiosity because it really does differ for every scenario. But what I will say is this, there are two types of contrast. Implied contrast and stated contrast. Stated contrast is when you share verbally both A and B explicitly. So, for example, saying something like this, "Most people solve their acne with Accutane, but I have an herbal remedy that does it three times faster." You're stating Accutane verse herbal remedy, so it's impossible to miss what that contrast is. The other type of contrast, which is way more subtle, is implied. And in this case, you say what the contrarian alternative is, but you don't reference the base because it's implied. People know what the base solution is. So for example, if I say if you want to solve your acne, this herbal supplement is eight times more effective. If the common viewer already knows what the baseline solutions are, nothing, Accutane, whatever they are, then you don't need to say it again because it's implied what their baseline understanding is. Essentially, it's your contrarian take versus the field of all other options. So you really have two options to create the contrast. You can go stated, which is way more blunt, A versus B, impossible to misunderstand, or you can go implied, which is a little bit more savvy and you don't really call it out specifically. Now, tactically, when you're writing hooks, typically the topic clarity comes in the first sentence, and then you set up that contrast in the following one to two sentences. This is why I consider hooks to really be like two to three lines. They're not always just a single punchy line. Sometimes you can achieve the clarity and the contrast all together in one line. And if you can, those are the easiest hooks that you can reuse. Again, if you want the full master class on how to do this tactically, and you want a bunch of examples of good and bad across every niche, and you also want a checklist to just follow every time you make hooks, I have that all in the hooks master class. It's linked below. All right, guys. That is all I've got for this video. As a recap, we covered the four main hook mistakes that you're making that are preventing your videos from outperforming. Those mistakes are delay, confusion, irrelevance, and disinterest. As always, please leave a comment below if you like this video, and just in general for feedback. - How to Create a Killer Hook (Impossible to Skip): Kind: captions Language: en If you want your videos to perform better, you have to learn how to craft a winning hook. Now, I've studied literally thousands of videos. And it turns out when it comes to hooks, most people struggle with the same four things. And the good news is these are all very fixable if you know what to look for. So, in this video, I'm going to break all four of those things down. The core mistakes you're making, and the exact tactics for how you can fix them immediately. By the way, I know this works because content is all I do all day long. I have a million followers. I've done billions of views. And I've grown two separate personal brands in two different spaces. So, if you use this video as a checklist when you're making hooks, I guarantee you will get more views and your videos will be impossible to skip. All right, the first hook mistake is a big one. It's called single subject, single question. It's actually very simple. In order for a hook to work, it only needs to do two things. One, it needs to focus the viewer's attention on a single topic. And two, it has to plant the same question in every viewer's head. If you have 50,000 people watch a video, the goal is that after the hook, all 50,000 of them are aligned and curious about the same thing. For example, if I started a video like this, here are the three ways I grew the most last year. Is that a compelling hook? Well, first, what do you think the subject of the video is going to be based on that sentence? Most people would say it's going to be about the ways I grew, some growth tips or lessons learned, but it's a bit vague and unclear. Some might think I meant mindset growth. Others might think I meant business [music] growth. Even others might think I meant literal muscle growth or even YouTube growth. And see that is a huge problem in lack of clarity because the way I wrote that assumed you would know what type of growth I meant. When you write hooks, you cannot assume the viewer has any embedded information before watching the video. And that is a huge mistake I see people make. If the set of yours is fragmented in what their understanding of the topic is, then a lot of them are going to be really confused when the next sentence you say doesn't connect to the previous one. And that confusion is really why viewers don't hook and they churn. They don't churn because they don't like you. They churn because the story you start telling stops making sense and they can't follow it. And so the lesson is the way you write the first couple sentences in the hook has to be unmistakably clear and focused on a single subject. Now, the other piece of this is the question that pops in the viewer's head after they hear your hook. Cuz we all know hooks are supposed to create curiosity, right? Well, the best hooks plants the same question in every viewer's mind. So, if we go back to the original example, here are the three ways I grew the most last year. What question pops in your mind after hearing that? Well, some might say, what are the three ways? I'm ready to hear them. Others might say, grew how? What exactly are you talking about when you say growth? And even others might say, who is this guy? Why should I care how he grew? Is that going to relate or help me at all? That's three different questions popping up in different viewers' minds, which means there are three different curiosity paths that viewers are going down. And again, twothirds of them are going to be confused when the next sentence doesn't connect. This lack of clarity in the subject and the curiosity is why your hooks are not hooking. Okay, so now I'm going to tell you how to solve for this. Imagine I wrote that example hook like this. These are the three best methods for business owners to grow faster on YouTube. Now, the subject is unmistakably clear. the methods for how business owners are going to grow on YouTube. And there's only one main question that should be in everyone's mind when they hear that. What are the methods? I'm ready to hear them. Tell me. See, by adding that clarity, we've narrowed the focus onto a single subject and a single question, which gets everybody on the same page for when we continue to tell the story from here. So, when I start the next sentence, everybody is following along. And I know this seems pretty basic, but like I said, this is the number one problem that the most people struggle with in all the videos that I've reviewed. people just are not clear enough in the way they frame their hooks. So, what are the specific tactics that you should use as a checklist when you're writing your hooks to make sure you're achieving this single subject, single question framework? For one, read the hook back after you write it and ask yourself this. Is it possible for someone to misunderstand the subject that I'm focused on? And once you're good with that, ask yourself, what question should pop in the viewer's mind based on hearing this sentence? The question should be something shock inducing that makes the viewer lean in. something like, "How is this possible? Is this real? Can you tell me more? I can't believe that. Is it true?" If you can't immediately identify what single question a viewer should have in their mind, then you need to rewrite the hook and go again. Now, one cheat code for accomplishing both of these things, the subject and question at the same time, is to just use a question hook. Literally ask the question in the hook that you want to plant in their mind. So, you might say something like, "How can a business owner grow on YouTube without spending 40 hours per week?" This achieves both the subject and question clarity at the same time. All right, hook mistake number two is the three hook misalignment. And you may have heard this before cuz I kind of pioneered it, but there's three types of hooks. The visual hook is what is shown on the screen. The spoken hook is what is said verbally by the creator, and the text hook is the text that's written on top of the visuals. If those three hook components are not perfectly aligned, the viewer is going to get confused and churn. So when you want to change count, you don't modify it directly. You call set count new value and React updates everything for you. Boom. Now your app remembers things. It's like giving your app a brain without needing to build Skynet. But what if you want your app to do something when that brain changes? Use Effect is like your app's personal assistant. Want to fetch data when a component loads? Automatically update the page title when a user logs in. That's use effect. Here's the basic setup. The first argument is a function, what you want to run. The second is a dependency array. If you leave the array empty, the effect runs only once when the component mounts. But if you put something inside, like count, it runs every time that value changes. This gives you full control over when your side effects happen. Forget to add the array. Congrats, your app just entered the infinite loop dimension. So yes, use effect is powerful, but handle it with care. Now, what if your app's data needs to be shared across multiple components? Passing props down four levels is exhausting. This is where use context saves your life. Crowd drilling is that thing where you pass data through five components just to get it from A to B. It's annoying, messy, and hard to manage. Use context fixes that. With context, you can share data across your entire app without passing props manually. It's like creating a shared data backpack that any component can reach into. Imagine a logged in user's data. Instead of passing it to every nav, sidebar, and profile card, just create a context. First, we create a context called user context, initializing it with null. Next, we build and export a custom hook use user, which will let us easily access the data from the context whenever we need it. Then, we wrap our components inside a user context provider and pass the data we want to share through the value prop. In our navbar component, we use the use user hook to access the user data we've shared. Now, we can access and use this shared data anywhere in our app without having to pass props down manually. This hook is essential once your app grows beyond just a couple of components. But wait, what if the logic you're using is the same across multiple features? That's where custom hooks come in. When your code starts looking like copy-paste chaos, it's time to level up. Custom hooks let you write reusable logic that looks clean, elegant, and actually maintainable. For example, in our use context setup, we created a custom hook, use user, to easily access the shared data across components. Want a hook to handle online status or form validation? You can build your own. You name it, extract it and reuse it wherever. It's like turning messy leftovers into a gourmet meal. So, here's what you just unlocked. Use estate for remembering data. Use effect for running side effects. Use context for sharing data painlessly. Custom hooks for organizing logic like a pro. Master these and you're no longer just learning React. You're building powerful scalable apps. The kind that shows up in portfolios, interviews, and real world projects. If this video helped you, hit that like button. It helps more than you know. - The Psychology Behind Good Advertising: Kind: captions Language: en It should come as no surprise that modern advertising as we know it, has shaped our society in many ways. A lot of our daily decisions and life choices are influenced in part by advertising itself. It’s become such a deep-rooted constituent of our established norm that a world without it would seem, frankly, strange "Like so many others, I had become a slave to the IKEA nesting instinct" "Uh, yes. I'd like to order the Erica Pekkary dust ruffles" "Please hold." This is because barely a moment goes by during our day when we aren’t bombarded with advertisements in some form or the other. Posters, billboards, flyers, TV commercials, and internet ads, all creep into our personal space and tell us what we should buy and who we should be. For now our only brief escape from our role as a potential consumer comes to us during sleep. But even this could possibly change one day. "Are you bored?" "Get Sky Go for your mobile" "Best entertainment and live sport" "When you want it and where you want it" What's important to know is that the purpose of advertising isn’t limited in its capacity to harass us into parting with our hard earned money. Advertising plays a traditional role in helping businesses reach prospective customers and vice versa. Without it we would not know where to look for a particular product or service we need. Perhaps without advertising we wouldn’t even know what we wanted in the first place. Yet in our present day technologically driven lives, the reach between producer and consumer has grown a lot smaller. With the numerous media platforms and channels available to us, a simple online search takes us to a list of providers able to satisfy our every want. Our dilemma today comes in the form of not knowing which product to choose from out of the many available to us. This is where good advertising comes into play. In a saturated market, subtle differences can make the distinction between the choice of one product over another. There are typically two modes of advertising that ad agencies and marketing gurus utilize. One focuses on the qualities of the product, while the other seeks to arouse an emotional response from the intended audience. The moment you start to think about advertisements that have stood out to you in the recent past, there’s a high probability that they incorporated the latter. And there’s a good reason for this. "Well gentlemen, I don't think I have to tell you what you just witnessed here" "I think you do" Why should you choose one product over another? That decision becomes easy when you develop an affinity with a particular brand. It could be something as small as an aesthetically appealing logo design. Something that resonates with you and feels calming. The right colours and appropriate typography all matched in harmony for a well packaged product. But advertising goes beyond a well thought out logo or attractive packaging. The most successful ad campaigns hardly say anything about the product itself but instead create a lucid atmosphere that evokes a strong emotion from its target consumer. These are the types of advertisements that we remember, talk about, and influence our purchasing decisions. Now, let’s take a look at the following two commercials about perfume: "Fragrances by Shulton" "The essence of precious scents caught in that precise moment of fulfillment" "Distilled with exquisite artistry for your every mood" "In four fragrances" "Here's the newest adventure in fragrances" "Escapade" "A blending of subtle French genius with a bold, vivacious, American touch" "To be lovely is to feel lovely when your fragrance expresses your gayest self" "So choose a gay adventure - choose Escapade toilet water" "Immediately, you'll feel lovely" "Why, you are lovely in that light and gay Escapade mood" "And remember your Escapade stick cologne to a new adventure, wherever you are" "Enjoy all these fragrances" "Friendship's garden" "Early American Old Spice" "Dessert Flower - At leading cosmetic counters everywhere" "Toilet Waters at a $1.25 and a $1.50, stick colognes $1" "Acqua di Gioia, the new eau fraiche" "Giorgio Armani" The differences between the two commercials are quite stark. The first ad for Escapade Perfume quite explicitly focuses on the product itself. They describe certain characteristics of the perfume while going on to talk about its application and effect on the user. And this is quite difficult to do when describing a product whose main selling attribute (smell) is not transmissible through Television. It almost seems absurd, but the second perfume commercial for Giorgio Armani does not even try in the least to directly communicate the features of their product. They rely solely on alighting particular feelings and associations with their perfume. In this case, we could assume that the directors behind the ad wanted to transmit the feeling of ethereal beauty. We see a woman who fits into our standard of high attractiveness in our society, frolicking through a rainforest in the midst of a storm. The only mention of the perfume is in the last six seconds of the one minute ad. So why do we care about the associations of a product, rather than the product itself? Good advertising helps us begin to answer one of the most fundamental questions of life – Who Am I? This is because when it comes to figuring out who we are and what we want from life, we usually struggle to find answers. A lot of this is existential and has to do with the fact that we’re born with no pre-established notion of what it means to be human. It’s up to us to figure that along the way. But making that decision isn’t easy. In fact, it’s a huge burden. Out of all the possibilities our lives can take, how can we decide who or what we should be? We have no inkling if the choices we make will turn out to be good or not. Yet, we are each tasked with the responsibility of deciding for ourselves and can only hope that we’ve chosen well. On the other hand, good advertising helps us build an identity by releasing the anxiety brought about by self-determination. It tells us exactly what choice to make by compelling us to buy a certain product. And once we have done so, we will be able to emulate the identity and characteristics that we have learned to associate with that product from a particular commercial or advertisement. "Advertising is based on one thing" "Happiness" "And do you know what happiness is? Happiness is the smell of a new car" "It's freedom from fear. It's a billboard on the side of the road that screams, with reassurance, that whatever you're doing, it's okay." "You are okay" Advertising that caters to our feelings, primarily resonates with our subconscious mind and not our conscious mind. It’s why we sometimes can’t rationally deduce our preference for a certain brand and our ability to pay a premium for a product we can’t tell apart from its competitors. If we are drawn to it simply because of what it evokes inside of us and the associations that come with it, then rest assured, the marketing department has done their research. What this means is that we need to start thinking carefully about the decisions we make even if it’s something as insignificant as purchasing a perfume. Good advertising feeds off both our insecurities and deficiencies as humans and makes us believe that we can mask them with a new and exciting identity. Make no mistake, the only thing you’ll be able to achieve is to diminish your anxiety in the short term. And of course, you’ll spend money on things you don’t need in order to quell a discomfort that needs to be addressed appropriately. Making authentic decisions that align with our best interests is no easy task and takes a lot of effort. Yet, we have to realize that losing ourselves into the illusions constructed by good advertising will not make our lives any easier. They will only detract us from accepting and being comfortable with who we really are and the givens of our reality. There is no point striving towards an ideal when perfection doesn’t exist. Accomplish this and you’ll be a much happier individual.

- How to Write a Hook and Engage your Audience: Kind: captions Language: en-US With the deadline approaching, Ken stares at his blinking cursor, unable to write a word. Why is it so difficult to write a captivating hook? Ken is not alone. So many students struggle with starting their essays, but in this video I'll explain the most common techniques you can use to write a hook. And I'll tell you the absolute best technique you can use, whether it's in an essay or a sales pitch. First, what is a hook and why do I need it? A hook consists of the first few sentences of your introduction that's used to captivate or hook your audience, so they want to keep reading or listening. A hook should be intriguing and related to the topic of the essay or speech so that your audience starts engaging with your ideas. Okay, but how do I create a hook? One option is to create a vivid description or tell a story. This technique engages your audience right away because they need to imagine the scenario you're painting with. Your words use vivid verbs to show what someone is doing and add only relevant details that will easily transition to the topic of your essay. When you can't think of a way to hook your audience, another option is to let someone else do it by using a quote. The quote should be from someone with authority on the topic you're writing about, and it should be something interesting that they say. Make sure it's not too long since you don't want it to run on and have the reader lose interest. And don't forget to cite your quotation. Another way to hook your audience is to start with an interesting fact or a statistic. The fact or statistics should be fairly unknown and something that may slightly shock the audience. Again, remember to properly cite your information. Another way to hook your audience is to ask meaningful questions. Many times students will ask a rhetorical question, but it's not always meaningful. Other times students will ask a question that just repeats the prompt in order to create a meaningful question. Think about what you'd ask your audience. If you want your audience to really care about your topic. What aspect of your topic could they connect with? Finally, the best way to hook your audience is to use the story technique and combine it with another technique. Why the emphasis on a story? Well, according to cognitive psychologist Jerome Bruner. He suggests that we are 22 times more likely to remember a fact when it has been wrapped in a story. Why? Because stories are memorable. Stories help us grab the gist of an idea quickly. The trigger or emotion as you decide which technique to use. Here's a list of do's and don'ts for writing hooks. First, keep it short and clear. Writing 1 to 3 sentences for your hook is ideal. Next, make sure your hook introduces and leads into your main topic. You don't want your hook to focus on a topic not covered in the essay. Another tip is to make sure you cite outside information in order to avoid plagiarism. Next, even though your hook is the first part, the audience reads. Try to write it last. It helps to have your argument established so you can think of an appropriate hook to draw in that audience. Finally, don't start with a dictionary definition. Definitions tend to be dry and boring and don't really engage audiences.

- 13 Powerful Hooks to Get More Views | Content Writing Tips: Kind: captions Language: en Some content and videos get millions of views, while others get very few. Why is this so? The difference isn't in the content itself, but in the first five seconds, the hook. What is a hook? How does it work? Watch the video in the comments to find out. And today, let's study important types of hooks. The first is the comparison hook. When we compare two things or people, the difference between them becomes clear to us, and this clarity helps us understand the message quickly and easily. This hook works in a similar way. Now, let's understand this using the example on the screen, where it's shown that most writers chase their clients. But smart writers attract them. This hook uses words like chase and attract to compare two ideas, creating a contrast. And this contrast attracts the reader to the content. A curiosity gap hook provides partial or incomplete information, creating a knowledge gap. This hook works just like the curiosity headline we read. Our brains crave closure. Therefore, when information is incomplete, it creates a sense of unease. To eliminate this suspense and unease, our readers read or view our content. As the example illustrates, a communication mistake can lead to people ignoring you. Here, we explained the problem and the result to the reader, but didn't disclose the mistake that created the problem. To fill this knowledge gap, their brain seeks further information, which increases the content's click rate. A quotation hook: When we use a quote from a well-known person as a hook, the audience's trust in the content automatically increases. For example, the example here is a quote by George Bernard Shaw. When people hear the names of George or Steve Jobs, they automatically pay more attention to your video or writing because they think that if someone from the greatest personalities said it, the content must be powerful. However, keep in mind that this hook should only be used when the quote is directly relevant to your topic and provides a clear meaning . If the quote is irrelevant, your points may be weakened. When content begins with an unexpected fact, data, shock, or surprising element, it is called a statistical hook or a surprising fact hook. This hook breaks the reader's expectations, and when an expectation is broken, the mind reacts suddenly. As explained in this example, the hook is explained. Did you know that most arguments don't arise because people disagree, but because they simply don't understand each other? So, this hook here breaks a common belief. It challenges a common belief that when an argument occurs, it means there's an ongoing feud between two people. When you explain that the real reason is a misunderstanding, they react. So, how can this be fixed? This is a surprising fact. This interruption instantly distracts intent, and people tend to listen or read attentively. The fifth one is the "imagine" and "scenario" hook. This hook is used to create a picture in the reader's mind. Imagine standing in front of 10 people. You're speaking. Everyone is listening to you in complete silence. There are no interruptions of any kind. As soon as you read this line, your mind begins to picture the scene . Meaning, a visualization begins. So, this kind of hook shows the viewer a dream. As soon as they visualize this scene, they develop an emotional connection to the content. Because they are now relating this topic to their own life, this hook creates an emotional bond and increases engagement. This hook is often used in motivational content, storytelling, and persuasive writing . A thought-provoking question hook is a question that immediately forces the reader to think. For example, "Why do people ignore you when you speak softly?" This question directly touches the reader's self-respect and personal experience. They immediately begin to delve into old memories, wondering, "Yes, this happened to me too." But why? Upon reading such a question, the reader pauses for a minute to reflect. This activates their thinking process and draws them into the topic . However, boring and predictable questions, whose answers are simply "yes, no," are not. They should be avoided because they don't create curiosity or deep thinking . Problem and Pain Point Hooks: Opening the content with a conflicting pain or difficult hook that the reader is also facing, they feel like this person is talking about me. Perhaps he has a solution to my problem . When the content starts with simple information or a real problem, we naturally pay more attention to the problematic element. Because the brain first notices the threat, discomfort, or problem. For example, if you are explaining a wonderful idea to someone, but the person sitting in front of you doesn't react, this silent rejection irritates us. So, this line highlights a real pain point. The reader immediately relates that yes, I have felt this way too, and reads the content to get rid of this pain. Definition: A redefined hook means defining a non-concept or topic from a new angle . We all have a set definition for everything. For example, we assume that someone who is successful must have a lot of money. When you break an old definition and present it from a new perspective, the reader experiences a shift in their mindset. They feel they are about to learn something deep and intellectual. For example, the example here explains that communication is n't about talking; it's about making others feel understood. However, most of us think that communication means speaking. But here it 's clearly stated that communication isn't just about speaking; it's about making the other person feel understood. When the leader reads this, their mind says, "I never thought of it that way." This perspective shift automatically increases attention and strengthens engagement. Personal story and anecdote hooks start with a relatable story or personal experience. For example, "In school, I knew every answer, but I was scared to read my hand." This line reflects a common feeling. Many people can relate to this situation because we often do, and this relatability boosts engagement. This type of hook makes the reader feel that they're not alone. When a story becomes relatable, it creates emotional safety and develops understanding. This is why people read or listen more attentively. Urgency and time-sensitive hooks: If you don't correct your communication habits now, they will become permanent. This hook conveys that if action isn't taken now, harm could occur. This means that this hook creates pressure and seriousness in the reader's mind, creating an urgency of loss. And we humans are more affected by the fear of loss than the joy of gaining. So, when you include the factor of time or permanent damage in your hook , the audience feels that it's very important to watch this video right now. Skipping this content now could ruin their future. A bold statement hook: A hook that makes a strong, confident, and sometimes controversial claim creates some tension in the reader's mind . When we challenge someone's existing belief, something they 've held since childhood or for a long time, they feel a sense of discomfort. To overcome this discomfort and understand your logic, they engage with the content. For example, we often think that those who speak loudly are confident. But this hook disproves this basic belief. Challenging a statement leaves them perplexed and wondering, "If this is wrong, what's right?" They click on your content to find the answer to this question . Prediction and Future-Based Hooks: People always want to be prepared for tomorrow so they don't lag behind. So, when you open content with a hook that suggests what's coming next , what trends are emerging, viewers are drawn to the content to learn more. For example, this example implies that in the next five years, something more important than marks will matter: communication skills. This line puts the reader on alert. They begin to think that in the future, not just good marks will matter; other skills may also matter. This future tension drives them to read the entire content. In a humor hook, we open our content with a lighthearted or funny statement . And when we laugh, it's like an eye break, reducing resistance. We see this in our everyday lives too. When egos between two people are at stake, they're often confused. If they don't, it's easier to talk to them and learn from them. This hook also works in a way that makes the viewer enjoy reading the content more. For example, I used to think I was speaking very clearly until my friend came and said, "I can't understand anything." Then I realized there's a big difference between speaking well and being understood. Everyone laughs when they hear this line, because it's happened to all of us at one time or another. The reader feels like they're just like me, and when they relate to the writer or creator, learning becomes much easier, and that's why they jump on the content. Like headlines, hooks aren't limited to blog or article writing. You can use them in YouTube videos, social media posts, emails, marketing, public speaking, blogs, Reels, and shorts . That's part of why he started gravitating toward graphic novels. They filled in those visual blanks for him. Suddenly, he could see what was going on, and that made all the difference. So, if your child has trouble following along or seems bored or lost with textonly books, this might be something to look at. Consider, do they imagine scenes as they read? Do they think in pictures? Or does their mind feel kind of blank when they try? And while we're on the subject, do you picture things when you read? This is actually super individual. Some people get full-blown movies in their heads, while others see more of a photo slideshow, and some people don't see anything at all. They hear a voice or they just feel the story instead. I'm a kind of fuzzy picture reader. I get a mix of scenes and snapshots, but they're not super crisp unless I really work at it. That's one reason I love seeing the movie version before I read. It gives my brain a little head start when it comes to visualizing the world and the characters. And even for kids who have that mental movie running, genres like fantasy and science fiction can really push the boundaries of their imagination. Having a movie as a starting point can fill in those gaps and make the story more inviting. And if this is something you want help building at home, send me a DM or shoot me an email. If there's enough interest, I'd be happy to put together a whole episode just on building that mental movie skill. All right, now let's talk about the whole read first or watch first thing because this question comes up a lot. Watching the movie first can actually help kids feel more confident about tackling the book. They already know the plot, they recognize the characters, and they have an idea of what's coming, so the book doesn't feel quite so overwhelming. Now, on the other hand, reading the book first can create a sense of anticipation and make the movie feel like a payoff, a little fun reward for sticking with the story. Honestly, there's no one-sizefits-all answer here. It really depends on your kid, the book, and the season of life you're in. Sometimes we read first, sometimes we watch first, sometimes we only watch, and that's okay, too. Shoot, we saw the Percy Jackson movies before we even thought about tackling the books. What matters most is that your child feels some sense of ownership. letting them decide whether they want to read first or watch first makes them way more likely to stay engaged. So instead of treating the movie like a shortcut or something to be avoided, you can actually use it as a bridge, a way to pull your kid into the story. You're not replacing the book. You're using the movie to make the book feel more accessible. And once you've done both, whether you read first or watch first, or if you did a little back and forth, this is a great chance to connect with your child through the story. You don't have to sit down with a worksheet or quiz them on character traits. Just keep it light and curious. You can ask them what was different between the two versions. Which did they like better? Do the characters look like they imagined? Was there anything that the book did better than the movie or vice versa? Or one more question that I really love. What do you wish the movie had shown more of? Don't even get me started on the Harry Potter series of books and movies. I could go on for days. Bottom line, these conversations can be a really natural way to build critical thinking by comparing the two versions. But you're not meant to be turning this into homework, just enjoy the story time together without pressure. Now, if you're looking for ideas to get started, I've pulled together some favorite book to movie picks based on age and stage. All right, first up for the younger kids. So, if nothing else, you can always start there. All right, now on to our growing readers. Those in second and third grade. You've got Charlotte's Web, The BFG, Judy Moody, and The Nots So Bummer Summer, The Bad Guys, How to Train Your Dragon, and Ramona and Beesus. These strike a nice balance between humor and heart, and they can really help bridge that transition into longer, more complex books. Last but not least, our middle-grade crowd. So, this is fourth through sixth grade. And finally, if you want to turn this into a little family event, try planning a book and movie weekend. You can read a few chapters during the week, then watch the movie on Friday night with pizza or popcorn, or do it in reverse. Watch the movie first to hook their interest, then read the book together, chapter by chapter. If you've got older kids that enjoy writing, you can encourage them to write a mini review or comparison highlighting what worked better in each, but only if they're interested. No pressure. This doesn't have to be a big deal. You're not sneaking broccoli into brownies here. You're simply meeting your child where they are and showing them that stories come in all forms and that they're allowed to enjoy them. So, if your kid loves screens, don't panic. Let's use that love to gently pull them back in towards books. Books and movies can absolutely work together, especially when we use them with intention, curiosity, and a little creativity. - What Makes An Editorial Lead Hook Readers In Journalism? - Journalism Explained: Kind: captions Language: en What makes an editorial lead hook? Readers in journalism. Imagine opening a newspaper or scrolling through a news website and being instantly drawn in. What makes you want to keep reading? It all starts with the first few words. That's the power of a strong editorial lead. It grabs your attention immediately and makes you want to know more. In journalism, especially when writing editorials, the lead is like a handshake that invites you into the writer's world. It's the first impression, and it needs to be clear and compelling. A good editorial lead clearly states what the piece is about. It tells you the main point or the argument right away. No beating around the bush. It should make you understand what the editorial is trying to say without reading too much. Think of it like a headline that also gives a sneak peek into the story. It's brief but packed with meaning. Engagement is key. The lead should make you curious or provoke a reaction. This can be done by asking a provocative question, sharing a surprising fact, or pointing out a current issue that everyone is talking about. For example, starting with a bold statement or a contrast can make the reader stop and think. It's about creating a sense of immediiacy and relevance. Relevance connects the lead to what's happening now. If the topic relates to a recent event or societal concern, it feels more urgent and important. The tone of the lead also sets the mood for the whole editorial. Whether serious, persuasive, or conversational, it should match the style of the publication and what the readers expect. When writing an editorial lead, consider starting with a strong statement that sums up your main argument. Or you could pose a question that makes the reader think about the issue. Sometimes a quick anecdote or example can make the topic more relatable. The goal is to make the reader want to continue reading and see your point of view. In specialized reporting and opinion writing, the lead is especially important. It determines whether the reader stays engaged or moves on. A clear, concise, and interesting lead can turn a simple editorial into a powerful piece that influences thoughts and sparks conversations. Remember, the first few words are your chance to hook the reader and set the stage for your message.

- First Page MISTAKES New Writers Make ❌ avoid these cringey clichés!: Kind: captions Language: en If you're a writer starting a new story, you know how intimidating it is to stare down that first blank page. Here's the scary truth. This first page is either going to make or break your book. Your reader is going to judge your writing based on what they see on this first page. So, if you don't pull them in, they're probably going to close the book and put it down and pick up something else. It's a lot of pressure. I know. That's why in this video, we are breaking down the dos and don'ts of writing page one. Common mistakes that new writers make that doom their book from the start and how to avoid these pitfalls so that you can make your opening page truly explosive and unput downable. Welcome back. If you're new here, I'm Abby and I help writers make their stories matter and make their author dreams come true. And if that's something you're on a mission to do, you're going to want to subscribe to this channel. I post writing videos every single Wednesday and I would love to have you here in the community. Okay, number one. Don't start with a cliche hook. A dramatic explosion, a character running for their life or waking up from a traumatic nightmare can work in some really specific instances, but most of the time these openings just feel like gimmicks designed to make the reader look. It's like screaming, "Hey, pay attention. This is important. This is dramatic." But if you don't show us why it's important, why it matters to any of the characters, we don't know why it's important to us. A random explosion or dramatic event won't impact the reader, won't make them care unless we see why it matters to the protagonist. You may have heard the writing advice that you should have something significant happening on page one. But significant doesn't necessarily mean a time bomb or a car chase or a character being held at knife point. Okay? It doesn't have to be life or death in order to draw us in. A dramatic hook might look something like this. The bomb went off at precisely 6:03 a.m. ripping through the quiet street and sending a fireball into the sky. Sarah jolted awake in her bed three blocks away, heart pounding. She stumbled to the window, the sky already glowing orange. Somewhere, sirens began to wail. Sure, it's loud and dramatic, but who is Sarah? Why do we care about her? Does it matter that she woke up to this explosion? Is this just an average Tuesday in her life? Or is this a significant day for some reason to her? Without context or emotional connection, an explosion is just an explosion. There's no character motivation, no personal stakes, no reason for the reader to care about what's happening. It's spectacle without substance. Do create an immediate story question. Starting with a story question is so much more powerful than a overly dramatic hook. A story question shows us that something immediately matters to the main character. And it matters to them because they have a personal stake in what's going on. You may have heard the age-old saying, "New money shouts, old money whispers." Well, the same thing applies for the hook on your first page in your story. A cliche hook shouts. A powerful hook whispers. For example, let's take that same story hook and make something different happen. At 6:03 a.m., the letter slid under Sarah's door. No signature, no return address, just five words in stark black ink. I know what you did. Sarah read it five times, her heart lodged in her throat as dark spots crowded her vision. Downstairs, a door thutdded shut. The messenger had vanished without a trace, but someone knew. And they wanted Sarah to know they knew. Why does this work? Because there's an immediate story question. What did Sarah do? Why does this other person know? Why are they leaving her a note about it? What's at stake if someone finds out? It matters to the main character. Therefore, it matters to us. No explosions, no cheap thrills, just the immediate tension of the moment, the internal conflict. What's happening inside the character? That's what makes your reader lean in and ask why? What is going on here? Mistake number two, don't start with a white room. Starting with a white room means opening with a vague abstract description or character's thought process with no context of where we are and what we're looking at. It's important to remember that when you first open a book, you're totally disoriented. It's like being blindfolded and then dropped into a new setting. And we take the blindfold off. Okay, what are we going to show our reader? You don't want your reader to get stuck on page one and then put the book down because they were too disoriented to continue. Here's an example of what I mean. She thought about running, about the way the air felt when she moved fast, like freedom wrapped in wind. The world was heavy, pressing in from all sides, and she couldn't breathe. Everything was too loud or maybe too quiet. She didn't know anymore. There's no setting. There's no hint of where she is, what she's doing, or who she is or what she's dealing with or anything that grounds us in a concrete place, time, and conflict. The reader is just drifting in this fog of abstract thoughts and emotions, and we have nothing solid to hold on to. Do anchor the reader in sensory detail. A strong, specific description of where we are and what we're looking at instantly makes a scene feel real. And remember, a little goes a long way. We don't need a ton of description to have a full sensory experience. Focus more on setting a mood rather than painting a fully detailed picture. Make it obvious by at least the second paragraph where we are and what we're looking at. For example, the bitter smell of smoke lingered in the air as Callum stepped under the yellow tape. Police lights pulsed against the brick walls, turning the alley into a stuttering wash of red and blue. He kept his hands in his coat pockets, eyes on the scorched doorway. It didn't look like an accident. And if he was right, then someone had gone to a lot of trouble to make it look like an accident. Here we are dropped into a tangible scene with sensory details. Okay, police lights, the smell of smoke, a scorched doorway. We know where we are and what we're looking at. There's an atmosphere and a mood, but there's also a clear story question. What is going on here? There's enough curiosity to keep us intrigued about what's happening without so much abstract, detached thought process that makes us feel we're in a white room. And kind of leading off of that is mistake number three, which is don't open with dialogue that lacks context. Snappy dialogue can be great. It can actually be a fantastic way to open your book and have this opening hook where we're plunged right into the middle of a scene. But if the readers don't know who's speaking, where they are, or why any of it matters, they'll be confused, not intrigued. For example, something like this. You're really going to do it. I don't have a choice. You always have a choice. Not this time. What if they find out? They won't. But what if they do? They just won't. Okay, trust me. By this point, your reader is practically screaming, "Who are these people? What are they talking about? Where are they? What is going on?" The vagueness doesn't make it mysterious. It makes it confusing and hollow. Without names, a setting, or a clue of what's at stake for these characters, we don't care. On the flip side, do leverage dialogue to show us what's happening and why it matters. Dialogue is a powerful tool when leveraged correctly. We can still have a bit of mystery and intrigue without feeling like we're floating in a void with no idea what's going on. So find that balance between sensory detail and dialogue to keep us grounded in the moment. Plunge us into the thick of the action and use the dialogue to sort of fill in the blanks of what's happening. For example, "You're bleeding," Maya said, reaching for his arm. Jace pulled away, wiping his hand on his jacket. It's not mine. They stood in the stairwell, one flight above the chaos, sirens blaring outside, footsteps thundering below, smoke curled under the exit door. Maya stared at him. What did you do? He didn't answer. In this case, we know who's talking, who they are, and we feel the tension in the conflict through the description in the sensory details and also through the dialogue. We're plunged into the middle of something urgent and the dialogue deepens the suspense rather than creating confusion. Before we move on to mistake number four, I want to quickly interrupt myself to tell you guys about a special live training that I'm hosting, continuing this discussion into storytelling techniques that actually hook readers on page one. This one is all about writing tension and suspense. As you've probably noticed, a common theme of today's video has been adding tension and suspense and intrigue and curiosity into your story so that your reader will continue flipping those pages. Because even if you hook them on page one with something intriguing, tension is really the secret ingredient that makes them want to keep reading and stay up all night. It's what transforms boring, meh writing into something bingeworthy and unput downable. That's why in this live training, we are going to explore how to inject real page turning tension into every scene, even the quiet scenes where nothing big is happening. The difference between real tension versus fake tension. How to hook your reader with tension on the first page so they're dying to know what happens next. My go-to framework for building tension from character desire, not just plot devices. How to raise the stakes without being melodramatic or over the top. and how to avoid the number one mistake new writers make when trying to add tension to their stories. We're going to break all of this down in the live training and I hope to see you there. It's happening Sunday, May 4th at 1:00 p.m. Eastern Standard Time. And don't stress if you can't make it to the live stream that day. You will still get access to the replay forever. And when you sign up for this live training today, you unlock access to my entire library of over 35 hours of in-depth live trainings diving deep into writing, editing, publishing, creating characters, marketing your book, and so much more. I can't wait to see you there. Save your spot at the link below this video. And let's get back into the page one mistakes. Mistake number four, don't try to be mysterious for the sake of intrigue. Like I keep saying, withholding everything, who the character is, where they are, what's happening, will make your reader confused, not curious. It's important to make your reader curious, yes, but there's a magic ratio, I find, with curiosity and reward. I see it as a balance of 2:1. So basically, we have twice as many questions as we have answers, but we're still getting answers. We are still getting rewards for our curiosity. When writers try too hard to be mysterious and cryptic, it can sometimes come across feeling like sloppy, vague poetry and not vivid, captivating pros. For example, they said the stars would whisper when it was time. Tonight, they screamed. She moved through the shadows, bare feet, silent against the stone. The blade was where she left it, ice cold and waiting for her. Everything was ending, or maybe beginning. It didn't matter anymore. She was ready. It's trying so hard to be cryptic and dramatic, but we have no idea who this main character is, where she is, what is she doing, and why are the stars screaming, and why does that matter? Even in a fantasy world, readers need at least a sliver of clarity before they can latch on to the conflict and care about it. On the flip side of that, do give your main character a very clear micro goal. Even something as simple as I just need to catch this bus gives us a sense that this character is moving towards something that matters to them. When we see the importance of this micro goal, then we're interested to see, are they going to accomplish it? Are they going to make it to that next step? Let's go back to that vague fantasy example and give our main character a micro goal that roots us in the conflict of what's happening. Mila pressed her hand to the temple door, praying it would open before the moon slipped behind the clouds. If it closed, she'd be locked out for another cycle, and the blade would be gone by morning. The emperor's guards were already on the ridge. She could see the torch light flickering through the mist. One minute, maybe less. She glanced over her shoulder, heart hammering. If they caught her trespassing after her brother's arrest, they wouldn't exile her. They'd execute her. We've taken something super vague and turned it into something really personal. The stakes are higher. We have political tension, personal tension, a do or die situation, a race against time. We still have a little bit of a mystery here, like what's the blade? Where is this temple? What is going on? Why does she have to get to it before the emperor's guards do? There's still those questions. We have curiosity, but it's grounded in concrete action and emotion. Show me enough to care, but leave out enough to make me curious. That's the golden rule. Mistake number five, don't frontload world building. If you're writing something like fantasy or sci-fi, resist the urge to info dump all the lore and the history of your world in that first page. I know you want to explain the magic system and the government and maybe the superpowers of your characters and how everything works, but nobody cares. Okay, that's the harsh reality. We do not care. We don't want to open that book and feel like we're immediately reading a Wikipedia page about your fantasy world and how it works and the natural laws that govern it. It's overwhelming and it is not grounded in a character. Therefore, we don't care about it. Here's an example of what I mean. In the time before the sundering, when the twin moons still rose as one, the kingdoms of Alenvar and Droai had not yet fractured beneath the weight of the great accord. The mage lords of the eastern reach still held dominion over the skyways and the elemental rights had not been outlawed by the ninth emperor's decree. But when the god veil cracked, splitting the realm route into seven plains, chaos swept through the veiled lands and cast the chosen into exile. Only then did the star saviors rise. There were at least seven proper nouns in that paragraph and zero mentions of actual characters. We don't know who we're following, why any of this matters right now, or why we should care about any of it. So, on the flip side of that, do show world building through action. This is my golden rule of world building and exposition. Let the world unfold naturally as your character moves through it. This is called exposition through action. We have an anchor point of this main character. We have a little bit of a hint of what matters to them and what they care about their internal conflict and we see them moving towards that micro goal on page one and they're moving through the world as they do it. And remember this world is ordinary to them. Okay? They're not going to hit the brakes to tell you how everything works. They're just going to move through it naturally. Challenge yourself to only mention the parts of your world that matter to your protagonist and what they're doing right now. So let's look at a better example. The guards at the border checkpoint didn't bother to look up as Ren slipped her forged travel slip onto the table. Good. That meant the charm was still working. She kept her head low, hood drawn, the scent of burnt copper clinging to her robes from the forge she'd passed on her way through the alchemy district. Just five more steps and she'd be across the threshold into Imperial territory, where magic was banned and where the name Ren Takara was still splashed across wanted posters. see the difference. We're thrust right into the middle of this fantasy world, but we're seeing it through the main character's eyes as she moves towards that micro goal, which in this case is crossing the border. We get hints of the world, travel slips, forbidden territories, magic charms, alchemy forges. We're setting the mood here, but all of it is relevant to what's happening right now to this main character. And number six, don't overdo the pros. Trying too hard to sound literary with a wall of overwritten metaphors and flowery language and literary sounding poetic pros is more likely to push your reader away rather than drawing them in. Opening a scene with vivid colorful detail can be great, but if it's just scenery with no connection to a character or conflict or anything that matters, your reader is going to be bored. I can't tell you how many books I have picked up that start something like this. The sun spilled its molten gold across the emerald hills, each blade of grass trembling with dew laced reverence beneath the kiss of dawn. A gossamer breeze meandered through the heather, rustling secrets older than time itself. The sky blushed a pale coral as if the heavens themselves were shy of waking. In the distance, the river sang its eternal lullabi to the slumbering earth. Sure, it sounds pretty, but who are we following? What do they want? What is their internal conflict? Why does it matter? This kind of detailed description might work as a poem, but not as the first page of your novel. When you get so enamored of the language itself and how pretty it has to sound, you forget to pull your reader into the story. Okay, that is the most important thing. If there's no character and no emotion, there's no reason to keep reading. So, on the flip side, do hint at your protagonist's internal conflict. Even if your main external conflict won't kick in until a few chapters from now, you should still be using this moment, this first page, to plant the seeds of tension for your character's internal conflict. Remember, they're dealing with something long before the story begins. So rather than hitting your reader with a bunch of flowery, overwritten pros, challenge yourself to peique their curiosity with a hint at the character's inner conflict. How can we drop a meaningful clue to what this character is struggling with internally in that first paragraph? For example, I was 29 minutes late to my ex-boyfriend's wedding, which in hindsight was the most punctual I'd been to any of his events. I sat in the back pew clutching a gift bag with a bottle of midshelf champagne and a card that said, "Congrats on your next bad decision." Technically, I wasn't bitter. I just hadn't planned on showing up without a date. This works because it has a clear voice, tone, mood, and already a situation that's brimming with tension and awkwardness. And the internal conflict is baked right into the moment. We have a main character who's clearly still struggling with unresolved feelings, maybe a little bit of denial, maybe a little bit of bitterness and resentment, and we already see that she's rife with internal conflict. There's no need for purple pros. We're already drawn in by the character and what she's dealing with internally. And hopefully we're curious at this point of what she's going to do next. So boom, there you have it. The top six cringey mistakes to avoid with that first page and what to do instead. - How to Develop a Hook for Your Book: Kind: captions Language: en - Your book needs a hook. You have to give your reader a compelling reason to read or listen to you. Curiosity might sell a celebrity memoir, but you have to give your reader a cold, hard, reason to buy. That's the hook, the outcome from the outcome, you offer. But what in the heck is that? Well, if you want some extra support, to figure out what you have to offer, this video is for you. (upbeat rhythmic beats) Hey there, I'm Julie, The Book Broad, founder of Book Launchers, a professional publishing services company, helping you write, publish, and promote non-fiction books. I'm also the author of three books, including "Self-Publish and Succeed." In that book, in chapter two, I reveal the single most important thing, every non-fiction book needs to succeed, (bell dings) a hook. And, that hook is something that speaks directly to your ideal reader, to their fears, their aspirations. It's picking up where their conversations with themselves at 2:00 AM, are leaving off. It's showing them that you can help them, and you know what they're going through. My favorite example to illustrate this, is that your book possibly offers a hair regrowth solution, but that's not your hook, (error alarm) telling them that you can make their hair grow back. Your hook is the dramatic improvement in your reader's dating life, after their hair is covering their head, and making them look 10 years younger. This means your reader isn't only a bald man, it is a bald man who is looking for love, or dating and not enjoying the people who wanna date them, and believing that it's the receding hairline that's to blame, or the person that lacks confidence because they don't like how they look, and they believe having hair is going to change them, their confidence, and their career, and their love life, as a result. Got it? What pain matters? Well, pain, like they're wasting time. Wasting time with the wrong people, wasting time not getting the results they want the first time, wasting time with diets that don't work. You get the picture. Apply that pain point to your reader group, and what you offer. So, if your story is inspirational, maybe you're going to have them stop wasting time worrying about what other people think, and finally, just, step into their truth and be themselves. Maybe, you're trying to write a book, but you're wasting time, wondering if it's any good, or you started to write, but you lose focus. That would be a great reason to join our 12 week course, "Self-Publish and Succeed." or to get support from a writing coach, something we also have, check it out, at booklaunchers.com. Wasting something is a big pain point. Another big pain point, is that what they're doing now, isn't working. They're trying things to get results they want, ease their pain, save money, grow their business, build their YouTube channel, book more speaking gigs, write their book, so they aren't thinking about doing something. They are doing something, but it's not working. They realize their strategy isn't hittin' the mark, and they're looking for another approach. When I wrote my first book, "More Than Cashflow," The audience was someone who had bought an investment property, or two, in real estate, but it wasn't going well. Or, they were trying to get a deal done, but they were struggling. The book offered a different approach to buy properties, that fit with their life goals, so they can enjoy their life as an investor, but it also, truthfully, deterred some people from ever trying real estate, and that's okay, too, because real estate investing is not for everyone. The reason it wasn't working for those people, though, is that the investment strategy they were trying, wasn't a good fit for them. Another pain point, besides wasting something, and strategy not working, is a financial pain point. Financial pain points, can be an aspirational pain point, like, they aren't making the money they want, or they aren't ready for retirement, or it can be a fear pain point. They're afraid of losing their money, or they're in debt and they're afraid of what's going to happen. Regardless, there's a financial pain point, to many, many books. But, knowing what's on the other side of the financial pain point, is where the hook is. Is it retirement funding, so that you can support your children to live life, on their terms? Is it getting out of debt, so that you break the cycle in your family? Is it saving for university, so that you can be a doctor and save lives like the person who saved you? And, finally, one more pain category to know about, is the human pain. And, this is big. It can be support, connection, communication, but connection and acceptance is a need we have, as humans. So, how do you help them get where they want to go, in this human pain category? And, remember, that it's not only getting them away from those things, it's what that brings them to. Or, you can focus on how you help them communicate their way to career success. Like Dan Fraser shares in his book, "Kickass Presentations," or Steve Multer's book, "Nothing Gets Sold Until the Story Gets Told." There's also other books, like, "My Heart Behind Bars," by Lorri Britt, where she shares her powerful and hard experience, having her son go to prison, and feeling the loss of her friend's community and support circle as they judged her, like it was her fault as a mother. Kids don't have to be bad, have bad parents, or live in bad homes, to suffer mental health breakdowns, addiction or incarceration. Everything can change instantly. And, if it's happened to your family member, you know the emotional chaos, and the feelings of losing control, that threaten your very survival. So, her book gives you a guide, to get through that human pain. By the way, I'm so proud of Lorri for sharing this story. It's really powerful. The human pain is a big bucket of pain to draw from, but, remember, you have to go beyond the pain, and remember what your reader wants on the other side of it, and why. It's as simple, but definitely not as easy, as that, for most authors. A hook is essential to sell your book.
