- Copywriting Examples: How To Write A KILLER HOOK In Your Sales Copy: Kind: captions Language: en Do you know what the single most important part of any copy is? Whether you're writing an ad, a landing page, a sales page or an email, if you can nail this, your copy practically writes itself. Any guesses? Keep watching. Hey guys, it's Alex and this week we're going to talk about the single most important part of copywriting, the art of crafting the perfect hook. In copywriting and marketing a hook is exactly what it sounds like, a concept or an idea that gets people interested in what you have to say and what you have to offer. So a good hook has the job of reeling in a prospect by getting their attention enough to take the next step. Because let's face it, it doesn't matter if your sales copy is the most interesting, engaging, well-written masterpiece on the planet, if you can't get your prospects' attention, does it even matter? We are in the attention and retention business first, which is why using a powerful hook in your headlines, subject lines or at the beginning of a sales or landing page is absolutely critical, no matter your niche, product or market. It's what the reader sees first and determines whether or not they'll open that email, read the next section or click an ad. So arguably, writing killer hooks is the most important skill you can develop in copywriting. It's what determines whether your copy converts or flops. When comparing copywriting to screenwriting, your hook is essentially the log line. That one big idea that determines whether or not you're watching that movie or that docu-series on Netflix this Friday night. Why do you think 34 million people watched Tiger King the weekend it came out on Netflix? I mean, sure, you could argue that they were stuck at home and they had nothing better to do. But the show is about a gay gun-toting operator of a tiger park who was charged with murder-for-hire. Yeah, that is a pretty good hook. A great hook makes people go wait, what? Oh, I gotta see what this is all about! But there's something I really want to make clear. This is not an invitation to use clickbait, which is something very, very different from a great hook. There's a lot of debate out there right now about what's considered clickbait and everyone seems to have a different definition. To me, it's simple, clickbait is an intentionally misleading hook or headline that leads to content that's irrelevant, provides no value or just straight out lies. Great hooks are still majorly click-worthy but they are relevant, lead to value, whether it be educational, entertainment or inspirational value and they do not mislead your prospects. I've said this several times and I'll say it again, always lead with value and use empathy and connection in your copywriting - and if you want more tips, techniques and tutorials that are working today, go ahead and hit that subscribe button below to join the global Copy Posse. Now in this video, I'm going to share five of my favorite Copy Posse-Approved hooks to grab and hold your customers' attention with nothing but powerful and precise wording. As I like to say, the right phrase pays. These five hooks are a sneak peek at my full list of proven and effective hooks that I teach in my copywriter coaching program at the Copy Posse Launch Pad. By the way, if you're interested and ready to ignite your freelance copywriting business, you can now get the recordings of this program which includes access to all the training modules, Q&A sessions, workbooks, guides, formulas and lots and lots of juicy bonus content. You can find out more about how to get your hands on that in the description below. Alright, now here they are, five powerful hooks that you can use to capture and keep attention. Now please bear in mind that these five hooks are not mutually exclusive. Often a great hook can utilize more than one of these concepts or angles. Let's start with hook numero uno - Threat, Warning and Pain. Now guys, I don't mean to start things off super intense but the heart of this first hook is primal. It's an old-school approach that still works today. Illustrating a threatening situation or an urgent warning or an unwanted pain that resonates with your prospects will likely get their attention. Science has proven that all decisions made by us humans are either to avoid pain or gain pleasure but here's the plot twist, people will actually do much more to avoid pain than to gain pleasure. The notion here is that you would likely act faster if you were say about to be attacked by a bear than if someone offered you a suitcase full of cash. Not that you have to get that intense in your copy but really think about the problems your audience is facing. Don't unnecessarily fear-monger or use clickbait, of course, make sure that it's relevant to your product and that it would lead your prospect to something that can actually help them solve their problem. And it goes without saying that this hook works well for a Problem Aware audience and you're hooking attention by speaking to that pain. So as an example, in this ad, Pacific Blue Cross used a stern warning to remind travelers of the high medical cost should anything happen to you during your vacation if you don't have the right travel insurance. And here's another one from ADT that shares that 26% of burglaries happen when someone is at home, urging you to take action to feel safe. And this ad also plays up a second type of hook and that is education and FYI. A great way to hook attention is to provide useful and relevant information that opens the loop and encourages your prospect to want to learn more. Besides, no one can resist a good little-known fact or a shocking, did you know? Using education or what I call the "FYI Hook" is a great way to appeal to prospects that have little awareness of your product or solution. Education is a great way to indoctrinate unaware leads. A great example of this hook is a series of posts by Acorns, a brilliant investing app that helps people invest their change. They use eye-opening findings and stats in their hooks to speak to their target audience, millennials. Now this ad may not be as shocking but serves as a great reminder of how our current education system really fails to teach us how to manage our finances. This ad however, sheds some light on a daily routine that far too many of us are guilty of, the amount of money we spend on coffee (chuckles). And that brings me to hook number three Confirm Beliefs. It's no surprise that people tend to respond or gravitate towards evidence or information that supports their existing beliefs. This gives your prospect a sense of validation and acknowledgement, that moment where you go, aha, I knew it or "oh my god, same!" This hook is also great for a Problem Aware audience. Those people that might not be aware of your product yet but they're experiencing the pain that your product is offering to solve. The best way to use this hook is to open with a powerful statement that confirms an existing belief but then pivot to present some new information that will get them to go, hmm, interesting. So here's a great example from Organixx. They spoke to women who were struggling with moodiness and irritability by validating what most of us already know that the cause could be hormonal imbalances. But then it goes on to share that this could also be the cause of insomnia, weight fluctuations or even dry skin. They confirm a well-known belief but then present new information based on this belief that makes their audience want to know more. Now be careful that the new information doesn't completely violate the existing belief or jump to a completely new paradigm that just doesn't make sense. There needs to be a believable connection. If it's too hard to swallow, you will have a hard time selling. Alright, now moving on to hook number four, Fear of Missing Out. Yes, I am talking about that anxiety-inducing feeling of being left out in a social situation. In the context of marketing, FOMO is really an opportunity to merge scarcity with social proof by showcasing the number of people who are already experiencing the benefits you offer, and therefore making your prospects feel like they are missing out. It's a good old fashioned "Everyone is doing it, so why aren't you?" The point here is to leverage social proof in an authentic and relatable way that resonates with the prospect and creates the desire for them to take action. For example, Blinkist, the app that summarizes bestselling books into 15-minute reports, does this very, very well with their headline. Millions of tech savvy intellectuals are using Blinkist to stay ahead of their peers and on top of their fields. And Live Recover, an abandoned cart recovery service, creates double FOMO by letting businesses know that they're missing out on recovering 21% of people who abandon their cart and also use the famous "who else" headline implying that other people are already using this service. Alright, now hook number five, Relevancy. There has never been a time when relevancy is more well, relevant to ensure the success of a marketing campaign. What is relevant to your market today? With the abundance of brands and solutions that are available and visible to your customers, especially in the digital world, relevancy is perhaps the best way to create a stronger and more meaningful connection between brand and customer. A hook that uses relevancy is one that takes into account current events, cultures or issues that your target audience can relate to, and of course connecting it to your product or offer. The goal here is not only get attention but do it in a way that makes your prospect go, "Oh, wow, you really get where I'm at." So think current events, pop culture, or trending topics on social media. How can you piggyback on these conversations and relate it to your product? This is where empathy can go a long, long way. In fact, it lies at the core of this hook. For example, during the 2016 presidential elections in the USA, Aspirin brand Excedrin was clever to poke fun at the political environment with the headline, 73% of Americans will have an election headache this year And hey, they can reuse it every four years. Alright and there you have it, five of the most effective hooks that we here at the Copy Posse love to use. Give me a thumbs up below if you found this video helpful. I hope it gives you some inspiration the next time you need to turn out some killer headlines or subject lines. Speaking of which, you can watch my video on How to Write Hot Headlines right here. Or you can check out my video on the Five Levels of Customer Awareness right here. Thank you so much for watching and subscribing. I will see you again next week. Until then, I'm Alex! Ciao for now.

  18. @f3rn4n2x3str3ll4: Since you were advocating for introspection, consider this:
Every post in social media can be seen as a response to the question “how to be happy?”.
Example: Your friend posts a travel picture. They just say something about what they experienced, in the caption, like: “I spent the whole night up and didn’t feel tired!”. But they were implicitly saying: “I was feeling like my daily routine was narrowing my view of the world and life, so I aimed to expand it with travel. When I traveled, I did all these things and this is how well it served my intended purpose”. Since no one is requesting your friend to be explicit about those 3 components (the problem/goal, the method they used to achieve that goal, and how well it worked) your friend doesn’t explain them explicitly. But everyone should be explicit about them. 
Why?
Because it would help someone else. If someone else had the same goal as you, they could see what worked for you, and if you evaluate that method very positively, they would compare your rating to the rating they give to the method they were trying so far or considering, and may try your method instead. Yes, maybe a “10/10” rating is subjective for everyone, but it would still give some sense of ”objective” measure of effectiveness.
So, everyone can say the components  explicitly, or social media could request you to fill in those 3 components for every post you make, so it’s easier for the software to find all posts that are describing how to reach a given goal, all the methods tried to achieve that goal, and all the ratings.
Now, social media could be designed with those components as the basis of the design. You could just login and search for a goal or create one if yours doesn’t exist, see the methods that exist to achieve that goal, which ones have been tried by people, and how people have evaluated every attempt. They could add nuance or extra details to their numeric review with an extra text field.
I was thinking of what would be the fastest way to implement such a social media nowadays, and my current conclusion is that it can be in a Discord server: each channel can be a goal, each post in a channel is a method, and each reply to a post is a review of someone’s attempt to use that method to reach that goal. Everyone can quickly find methods to try and they can leave their reviews after giving an honest attempt. If the nature of some attempt really requires a person to update their evaluation or append to it, it would be best that they update the same review instead of creating new ones that are harder to link together. What they can do is start a review, grab a link to the reply they just made, and save it as a bookmark so they can come back to it later. I created such a Discord server but haven’t shared it with anyone yet. No reason for it, just doing something else.
More broadly, this system leverages the core of what looking for truth is: if you really want to reach your goal, you want to know what the TRUE method to reach your goal is. Why? Because reality works a certain way. I’m not implying it is a limited way. It just works in some way. You want to operate in the way reality actually works. 
So, when using this system, users are not distracted by prejudices they may have regarding where a method came from. Even though someone may suggest a method that was originally from a tradition, philosophy, body of work, experiment, culture, religion, etc., the method is simply presented as the essence what it is: a standalone method to reach the goal you chose to reach, instead of one part of many others that you must ascribe by to reach the goal someone else tells you you should reach. That is, the prejudice may come from the fact that someone is offering you more than what you need, e.g. “join my culture, do all these things, and then you will get this goal” so you wonder "do I need all that?", and from the fact that someone is offering you to reach a goal that you haven’t chosen yourself that you want to reach, e.g. if someone offers you a method to feel the whole universe as part of you, you may not be sure if you want it when all you want right now is not to feel angry with someone.
What do you think?

relevant to your audience tailoring your content to special occasions can boost engagement 7. use email marketing platforms insights many email marketing platforms offer insights into the best times - The 6-Scene Pattern Bestselling Authors Use to Hook Readers: Kind: captions Language: en You've heard it before. Every scene must go the next. It sounds clever, promising, even. Some people even wrote hundreds of pages pretending that's all it takes to be a so-called story genius. But let's be honest, if that were all it took, everyone would already be a best-selling author. Go and effect alone won't save your story. What matters here is which kind of scene is causing the next and in what order. Bestselling authors and top screenwriters understand this. The chain isn't random. It's driven by six distinct types of scenes. each one opening a very specific fork in the road for your characters. And those forks aren't interchangeable. They unfold in a deliberate progression that forces your characters to face parts of their internal conflict. So, let's start at the very beginning with the first type of scene, the inciting incident. Obviously, this isn't an inciting incident in the traditional sense, the one that kicks off your story, but it's the one that sets off carefully designed progressions known as sequences. Sequences are one part of the storytelling frameworks that have developed called the story pillars method which has received an overwhelming amount of success among fiction writers. It was designed to build on what already works and to fill the gaps where most writers are usually left in the dark. So, if you'd like to dive deeper into the full method, make sure to subscribe. Right. So, every sequence begins with an inciting incident, a scene that shakes the ground beneath your character's feet and destabilizes the current status quo. whether it is your protagonist or simply the POV character in focus. Speaking of which, sequences are structured a tad differently depending on whether your story follows a single protagonist or multiple point of view. But don't worry, we'll get to that in a minute. For now, let's look at a sequence from one of my favorite TV series, Desperate Housewives. In this sequence, we follow Susan, a single mom hiding a pretty dark secret. She accidentally sets her neighbor Brit's house on fire. And Edy isn't just a neighbor. She's also Susan romantic rival. Both women are interested in the new guy on the street, Mike Delino. During the chaos of the accident, Susan drops a measuring cup without realizing it, which is later found by another neighbor, Martha Uber. What triggers the sequence is when Martha eventually realizes that the measuring cup belongs to Susan. So, the inciting incident scene is when Martha visits Susan. She shows up with a pie. Polite, even generous on the surface. >> Mrs. Hoover. >> Hello, Susan. I made you a pie. >> Wow. Why do I need a motive to do something nice? >> Until Martha finally accuses her of setting Eddie's house on fire and pulls out the measuring cup as evidence. Susan denies it, but things quickly begin to escalate, pushing us straight into the second type of scene, the progressive complications. This is where things get messy for your characters and tension starts stacking up. One complication can work, but stacking escalating challenges makes your protagonist's world increasingly unstable and far more immersive for your reader. These complications can be external things happening around them or internal shifts in their thoughts, feelings, or gut instincts. Back in the spread's wives, we see the stakes climb pretty fast. After denying Martha's accusation, Susan runs into her at the grocery store. >> You shouldn't be rude to me, Susan. Your secret is not an easy burden to bear. That insurance company is putting Edie through hell. But still, I've said nothing. Well, >> and the longer it takes for her to get payment, the longer she'll be staying with me, eating me out of house and home, using up my hot water. >> Martha hints that if Susan doesn't pay for her groceries, she'll turn her in. It's blackmail and Susan gives in. Sooner or later, all that pressure that you've piled on your characters will snap. Which brings us to the third type of scenes, the turning point. This is the twist that drives the sequence in an irreversible direction. It forces your protagonist to confront the very dilemma set in motion by the inciting incident scene. A choice between two or more paths, each carrying real consequences for your characters. In other words, what started the sequence as disruption now hardens into decision. In Desperate O's Wives, the turning point hits when Susan comes home to a voicemail from Martha. This time demanding $600 to replace her broken water heater. >> I need to talk to you. My water heater just burst and it's going to cost me $600 to get a new one and I can't afford that. The blackmail has escalated far beyond groceries and Susan realizes that if she doesn't act, things will only spiral. That realization pushes us into the next type of scene, the crisis and contemplation. Quick question while we here, and feel free to answer in the comments. I was wondering if you were already structuring your story using sequences or if this was a new way for you to look at your draft. So yeah, let me know in the comments. All right, so the crisis and contemplation scene is where the emotional weight of the inciting incident scene finally lands. If you're anything like me, you've probably agonized here, debating what your character would really do, because acting will cost them something, but so will doing nothing. In Desperate Housewives, there are actually two crisis and contemplation scenes in this sequence. First, Susan tells her daughter the whole truth about the fire and Martha's blackmail. This leads to a dialogue where Susan says that she's considering turning herself into the police and hoping that they understand it was an accident. But her daughter, Julie, points out the consequences. Doing so would mean losing custody of her. >> You can't do that, >> Julie. I don't think they'll throw me in jail. I mean, it was an accident. Dad won't care if it was an accident. You know, he'll just use this as an excuse to reopen custody. In the second scene, Susan and Judy wait another option, breaking into Martha's house to retrieve the measuring cup. Susan hesitates since it means involving Judy in a break-in, but Julie plays devil's advocate. Technically is not theft since the measuring cup is theirs to begin with. After contemplating the costs of each option, your protagonist eventually makes a choice and that decision launches the next type of scene, the climax. This is where the choice turns into action and the plan plays out on the page. In Desperate Housewives, Susan and Judy wait for Martha to leave, stage a Frisbee game on the street, and throw it into Martha's garden as cover for Julie to sneak in and retrieve the measuring cup. And once the plan has played out, there's still one final step because every sequence needs to show us not just the action, but the consequences. It's that closing scene that reveals what's changed and whether your character's new normal is stronger or shakier than before. And that final scene type is the resolution. The resolution scene is where we see the consequences of the climax, the ripple effect of the choice your protagonist made. It marks a clear before and after both externally and internally. And it closes the sequence by revealing a new status quo, even if it's temporary. In Desperado's Wives, Martha visits Susan again, but this time everything has changed. Suzanne is waiting for her outside, symbolizing that she won't let Martha invade her home or her personal space again. >> You took it, didn't you? >> Good evening, Mrs. Hooper. >> It's my own fault for not hiding the cup. Obviously, if you're capable of arson, I should have known you'd be capable of breaking and entering. >> I don't know what you're talking about, Mrs. Hooper. >> And unlike at the beginning, Susan no longer denies that the measuring cup was hers. I suppose you destroyed it. >> Again, I don't know what you're talking about, but yeah, I did. >> So, when designing sequences for your own novel or when revising your draft, ask yourself, what disruption launches this sequence, and how does it reframe your character's status quo? How will the next scene keep raising pressure, stacking new costs, obstacles, or details that make the situation harder to escape? What scene makes it impossible for your protagonist to ignore the problem? What scene will show the characters weighing the options and the unavoidable consequences of each? What scene shows the chosen path being played out on the page? And finally, what scene shows how the character's status quo is now different from the opening of the sequence and how that change echoes forward into what's next. Now, I get asked this all the time. If you've got multiple POVs, do they all follow the same sequence structure? The short answer is no. Each point of view carries its own chain. But let me show you what that looks like. In a multiplay story like Desperate Housewives or even Game of Thrones, each character runs on their own internal sequence, meaning their own inciting incident, progressive complications, turning point, crisis and contemplation, climax, and resolution. If we start simple, here's what that can look like. Imagine chapter 1 follows POV1. That could be the inciting incident of sequence A. Chapter 2 switches to POV2, and that's the inciting incident of sequence B. Then chapter 3 returns to POV 1 with a progressive complication scene for sequence A. Chapter 4 switches back to POV 2 for a progressive complication scene in sequence B and so on so forth. But in practice, it's rarely this neat. Sequences don't all move at the same pace when POV might need several progressive complication scenes before hitting a turning point scene, while another could be ready to escalate much faster. So you could end up with something like this. Chapter 11 is the inciting incident of sequence C for POV1. While chapter 12 jumps straight into the turning point scene of sequence D for POV2. The key idea is this. Each POV still follows the same internal order of scene types. Those chains might whiff together in your novel, but each one needs to stand on its own as a complete sequence. So there you have it. Sequences and not just cause and effect, but the deliberate chain that actually makes your story work. You can use them to fasttrack plotting from scratch or if you're revising, you can use them to spot missing scene types that weakened the flow. Once your sequences are solid, the next step is to master the scenes inside them. I've made a full breakdown on that which you can watch right here. And if it's not ready yet, then you'll find here my deep dive on dialogue instead where I break down the Martha and Susan scene that kicked off this sequence. Writers have said that video made dialogue clicked for them like nothing else before. I'm Julian Mlet. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next one.

  1. @writerLadyLiAndre [6 likes]: The sequence you're describing is what I use for the act structure. In three act structure,  the first act is the fear phase - fear is usually what prevents a character from moving forward across the Threshold. The second act is the learning phase where, through a series of "tests", the character comes to understand the challenge. After the Ordeal, they take the Reward gained and move into the third act - the proof phase. The final climax of the story is the proof that the character has either changed, or changed the story world. Sometimes both. Each act follows the sequence you described. In my epic novels, each chapter also follows the same sequence, which I call journey steps. I originally found the pattern accidentally as I wrote my first book. Shortly after that, I encountered Campbell's Hero's Journey. But I've come to realize that a novel is a collection of interwoven journeys. By using journey frameworks, I never have "sagging middles" that so many YouTube authors seem to worry about. You just need to make sure your story has enough journeys to support the length you are aiming for.

- I Analysed 100 Opening Lines. Here's What Makes Readers Obsessed: Kind: captions Language: en Over the last 3 months, I have developed what you might call an unhealthy obsession with opening lines. I've analyzed over a hundred opening lines from best-selling novels. Not just any novels, books that readers couldn't put down. Books that spawned fandoms. Books that people stayed up until 3:00 a.m. reading. Why on earth did I do this? Well, I wanted to answer one simple question. What makes an opening line so compelling that readers become obsessed? Here's what I discovered. Most writing advice about opening lines is completely wrong. People tell you to start with action or dialogue or a mysterious statement, but that's not what the data shows. After analyzing 100 bestsellers, I found four specific patterns that turn casual browsers into obsessed readers. And none of them are what you'd expect. Let me tell you why I started this experiment. Last year, I was working with a client. Brilliant storyteller, incredible plot, characters to die for. But her opening line was killing her book. Beta readers weren't hooked. Early reviewers were bouncing off in the first paragraph. Even her mother had said she wasn't sure about the beginning. We rewrote it using one of the patterns I'm about to share with you. The result, her book launched to rave reviews, hit bestseller lists within 2 months, all because of one sentence. Same story, same characters, completely different opening line. And that's when I realized opening lines aren't just important. They're everything. Now, before I dive into the patterns, let me be clear about something. I didn't analyze random opening lines. I specifically chose books that created obsession. Books where readers immediately devoured the entire series. Books that launch careers. Books that people still talk about years later. Because there's a difference between a good opening line and obsession creating opening lines. After studying a hundred of the best, four patterns emerged, and none of them are what the writing guides teach you. Pattern one is the emotional contradiction. This is a pattern I've not heard anybody talk about. Most writers think opening lines need to be dramatic or mysterious. But the most obsessive openings create what I call emotional whiplash. They set up one emotional expectation, then immediately subvert it. Here's an example of what I mean. All children except one grow up. This is how JM Barry opens Peter Pan with what seems like a comforting universal truth. But that exception, except one, immediately creates unease. It's an emotional contradiction. You have comfort and uncertainty. The pattern works because it creates cognitive tension. Our brains don't like contradictions. We keep reading to resolve the conflict. And so here is how to use it. Start with a statement that seems to point in one emotional direction, then add a detail that pulls it towards the opposite emotion. An example would be, "Jess had always been lucky in love until the morning she found her husband's other wedding ring. Starts with happiness, ends with betrayal, instant emotional whiplash, and instant obsession from your readers." The second pattern that emerged was the intimate universal. This one surprised me. The most obsessive opening lines don't start with big dramatic events. They start with small, deeply relatable moments that feel universal. But here's the key. They make the universal feel intimate. Like the author is speaking directly to something you've experienced, but never put into words. It was the best of times. It was the worst of times. Dickens isn't talking about specific events. He's capturing that feeling that we all have that life is simultaneously wonderful and terrible. Universal experience made intimate through specific language. And here is another. If you really want to hear about it, the first thing you'll probably want to know is where I was born and what my lousy childhood was like. Salinger opens catcher in the rye by acknowledging something universal, our curiosity about other people's origins. But he makes it intimate by having Holden speak directly to us. The pattern works because readers think this author gets me. And here's how to use it. Find a small universal human experience, then present it in a way that feels like a personal confession. Everybody lies about their first heartbreak, but I'll tell you the truth about mine. You can see the universal experience heartbreak, but it's made intimate by the personal confession. Readers will lean in immediately. The third pattern that emerged was something that I call the temporal disruption. This pattern broke my brain when I discovered it. The most obsessive opening lines mess with time. Not in obvious ways. It was the year 2087 or once upon a time. They create subtle temporal confusion that makes readers feel slightly offbalance. Another example would be last night I dreamt I went to Manderly again. Daphne Dmorier opens Rebecca by placing us in three different time periods simultaneously. We have last night, the recent past, the dream, which is timeless, and again, which is the distant past. Our brains have to work to orient ourselves. We keep reading to find stability. And another example, it was a bright cold day in April and the clocks were striking 13. Orwell starts 1984 with a date that feels normal and then adds an impossible detail. This temporal disruption creates unease without readers understanding why. We don't know when we are in the story. And here's how to use it. Play with verb tenses. Mix past and present. Reference future events in past tense. An example would be, "Tomorrow I wish I hadn't opened that door, but today I can't help myself." This creates temporal vertigo that keeps readers reading. If you want help crafting an opening line that uses these patterns effectively, one that hooks agents and readers from sentence one, this is exactly something we can help you with in our editorial services as well as editing your entire book and of course publishing it. There are links in the description below. The fourth pattern that emerged was something called the false certainty. This is probably the most sophisticated pattern, and it's the one that separates good opening lines from legendary ones. The most obsessive openings sound completely certain about something that's actually uncertain. They present information with total confidence, but plant subtle seeds of doubt. Here is an example. It was the day my grandmother exploded. This is how Ian Banks opens the crow road with what sounds like a definitive statement, but as you read, you realize exploded might not mean what you think it means. False certainty creates trust and then immediately undermines it. So here's another example. They say in the moment before you die, your life flashes before your eyes. Sounds like the narrator knows something definitive about death, but the phrase they say immediately introduces doubt. Who are they? How do they know? Can we trust this? And this pattern works because it exploits a cognitive bias. We trust confident statements, but we're also curious about uncertainty. False certainty gives us both simultaneously. Another great example is I am an invisible man. This is how Ralph Ellison opens invisible man with what seems like a clear statement of fact. But what does invisible mean? Does he mean this literally, metaphorically, socially? The certainty is actually complete ambiguity. And here's how to use it in your own writing. Make a definitive statement about something inherently uncertain. Use confident language about ambiguous concepts. So, let me give you one I cooked up. The thing about dying is that it's surprisingly inconvenient. This sounds certain, but actually raises more questions than it answers. Perfect false certainty. So, why do these patterns work so well? After analyzing a 100 opening lines, I realized something important. Obsessive opening lines don't just hook readers. They actually rewire their brains. Each pattern triggers a different neurological response. Emotional contradiction creates cognitive dissonance. We need a resolution. And the intimate universal activates mirror neurons. We feel understood. Temporal disruption engages our spatial reasoning. We need to find that orientation again. And full certainty triggers curiosity. We need clarification. All four patterns make reading feel necessary, not optional. You're probably now wondering, does your opening line create obsession? Well, here are four questions you can ask. Does it create emotional tension? Is there a contradiction? Does it feel personally relevant? That would be intimate universal. Does it disorient the reader slightly? Temporal disruption. And does it raise questions while seeming definitive? If your answer is no to all four, well then you need a new opening line. If you answer yes to even one, well then you're on the right track. If you answer yes to multiple patterns, sounds like you are well on your way to creating an opening line that will spark obsession in your readers. Now, let me show you these patterns in action. Before Sarah walked into the coffee shop and ordered her usual arte boring, no patterns, no obsession. But if we improve this, it would read something like Sarah ordered her latte for the last time, though she wouldn't realize it until her husband called with the news. This of course has an emotional contradiction because you have the usual routine versus life-changing news. You have temporal disruption, present action, future knowledge, past realization, full certainty from last time, but then you have vague news. And so these patterns in one sentence create instant obsession. Ultimately, obsession isn't created by drama. It's created by psychological tension. The best opening lines don't tell us what happens. They rewire how we think about what might happen. They make reading feel urgent, necessary, and inevitable. Your opening line isn't just the first sentence of your book. It's the reason readers become obsessed with your story. And now you know the four patterns that make it happen. Use them wisely because your readers are waiting to be obsessed by your writing. And you just have to give them a reason. If you want help crafting an opening line that uses these patterns to hook readers from word one, check out my editorial services in the description down below. And I'd love to hear from you in the comments. Which of these patterns are you going to try first? And even better than that, I'd love it if you put your first lines in the comments down below so that we can work on them together, improve them, and see if we can create some obsessive first lines. - How to Write a Perfect First Line (18 Examples!): Kind: captions Language: en Your first line is perhaps the most important in the entire story. It has a critical job to grab our attention and make us want to keep reading. But too often writers open their stories with a bland factual statement like it was a sunny day in Phoenix. Okay. And so what your first line has to make us curious to continue with the story. So, to help you nail your first line, today I'm going to do a live workshop of opening sentences submitted by you from your current drafts. I sent out a call for submissions to the premium subscribers of my newsletter, Chapter Break, and I got an incredible amount of responses. I'm going to read through each of the examples, then talk about whether I think it's a strong opening line as is, or if it's weak, how I might edit it to make it more effective. Stick around to the end because after we've gone through all the examples, I'm going to pick my top three favorites. Here's opening line number one for a literary thriller. The valley was innocent. I like this opening line. There's a bit of personification here in labeling the valley as innocent because of course a valley is not something we consider having human traits. But because this is a literary thriller, I think that suits the genre well. Of course, it also leads us to wonder why the narrator has to call out that the valley is innocent. Has it been accused of something? And if the valley is innocent, then who is guilty? My only note for this opening line is that we should quickly learn what the valley is in this context. Otherwise, we might be disoriented with this personification. So, as long as those answers are sorted out quickly, this could be a strong opening. Here's opening line number two, which is for a magical realism novel. Eduardo turned around on the bar stool to watch the woman on stage singing karaoke and was immediately bumped, spilling his rum and coke. So, the passive voice in this sentence was immediately bumped makes it sound a bit grammatically clunky and it would be stronger if we knew who was bumping Eduardo. While I do appreciate that the author centers us in immediate action and sets the scene of the karaoke bar, I wish we got a bit more insight into how Eduardo is feeling about his situation and where he is. As written, it reads more like just a factual statement than something coming from within Eduardo's perspective. I'd encourage this author to find a way to maybe weave in some of Eduardo's subjectivity and address that passive voice. Here's opening line number three, which is for an adult horror fantasy novel. A body tumbled toward the sea. This does immediately introduce a mystery. Whose body is it? But I wonder if we might get a few more telling details about that body to peique our interest even more. It's also difficult to tell if the body is lifeless or if this is a person swimming, for instance. This opening line also has a more distant perspective. It reads like omnisient narration rather than close third person. So, I question whether we should maybe be within a specific character's mind and body in this moment where they're observing the body tumbling toward the sea. Certainly not a bad opening line, though. Here's the next opening line, which is for an adult romanty novel. If beauty was a currency for women to procure a husband, Princess Myra was a popper. I like this opening line because it immediately tells us something about the character Princess Myra in an intriguing way. Rather than just saying she was unattractive, we use this comparison to currency, which is super interesting. And because this is adult romantic, maybe it also gives us a hint of the world that we're in. The phrasing for women to procure a husband almost gives me the vibe of Regency England. So maybe there's some of those elements coming into this fantastical world. There's also an immediate sense of tension created because we sense that Princess Myra needs to perhaps procure a husband but can't because of how she looks. And maybe that will be a tension that we see carried throughout the story. Overall, I like this opening line. Here's the next opening line for an adult comedic mystery. The world believes I'm dead. To me, this is a strong opening line because it immediately raises the question, why does the world believe they're dead? We want to learn more, which is exactly what you want your opening line to do. I like how short and punchy it is, too. It really gives us no choice but to read the next sentence. Here's the next opening line for an adult speculative thriller. The 3:00 a.m. light in this test lab was low. So, this opening line reads to me like a static description of the scene, which isn't necessarily that intriguing. We are curious to know why the character is in the test lab at 3:00 a.m. because, of course, that's quite late to be working in a lab, but I'd encourage the author to consider directing our attention to maybe some other elements beyond just the light being low. Is there the sound of glass breaking? Or does a light go out suddenly? This is another situation where the author could center us in the POV characters mind and body a bit more, which would likely make for a more engaging sentence. For example, maybe they convey their exhaustion or their commitment to finishing this experiment. There's definitely some interesting potential here. Here's the next opening line from an adult steamy romance novel. Cole Castile barged into his former fiance's bridal shop, clutching the industrial strength garbage bag in one fist. the last of her things stretching the heavy plastic. I like this opening line because it immediately places us in the scene and tells us quite a lot about the characters in very few words. We know that these two characters have just broken off an engagement. We know that the female character owns a bridal shop and we know that the male character is getting rid of her things. My one suggestion here would be to go even further with providing us more subtle character detail by naming one of the items that is stretching the plastic. Rather than just saying the last of her things stretching the heavy plastic, what if it was her cat tree stretching the heavy plastic or her mother's antique vase stretching the heavy plastic? Including a specific item there will give us even more detail about the fiance character. Here's the next opening line from an adult fantasy novel. Idrawa drew in a ragged breath. This one doesn't give us enough setting detail or enough characterization to really understand the context and therefore what to make of this ragged breath. As a result, it reads more like just a factual description and isn't all that intriguing. Try to indicate here what is it that's causing Idraa to breathe raggedly or what thought is passing through her mind as this is happening or where is she? There are different ways you can provide just a bit more context but that will go a long way in making this more intriguing. Here's the next opening line for an adult thriller. Shall we burn them all? Father the rectory helper asked as he leaned forward to get a better look from the oil lamps light. I generally don't love opening novels with dialogue because we tend to need a lot of context to understand what's going on, but I don't hate this one, honestly. That's because the author gives us a good amount of detail in the dialogue tag. In this case, we know it's the rectory helper speaking, which tells us not only who is present in the scene, but also where we are physically. We also know that the other character in this scene is the rectory helper's father, which is helpful. So, the author does a good job giving us context here. That said, I really wish I knew what them all was referring to because otherwise I don't understand the stakes of burning them. It sounds severe, but they could just be burning old receipts for all I know. Of course, we'll probably learn what this is referring to in the next sentence, but the author might consider bringing it into this sentence with the section as he leaned forward to get a better look. What is he looking at? that would tell us a lot more. So, those questions should be what the sentence focuses on. Here's the next opening line from a work of women's fiction. But this opening isn't quite working, and I'll get to why. Now, let's read manuscript 2, which is contemporary middlegrade. Howard and Sasha were going on an adventure, or so their parents had told them last Tuesday when they'd announced the family holiday this year was to Welchmouth on Sea. Sasha thought it sounded suspiciously like being trapped in a car for 4 hours with her annoying little brother. We're going to the seaside. Sasha's mouth turned downwards. The sea was that salty pool you couldn't swim in without mom and dad there. Yep, we've got a whole week to look forward to. Howard looked a lot happier. Awesome. I'm going to build the biggest sand castle and it's going to have a moat and a drawbridge. and his mother and father gave each other a smile, the same slightly wobbly smile they've been giving each other for a while now. "I have it on good authority that there's an excellent fish and chip shop just next to the inn. And there's also spending money. You two will be completely sick of ice cream by the end. I guarantee it," said Dad. Sasha rolled her eyes. "But Dad, I wanted to see my friends. How am I supposed to have any fun at a boring old inn? You'll just have to make your own fun, miss. She crossed her arms and huddled up on the backseat of the car, looking like a miniature storm cloud of thunderbolts and all. This writer has a nice handle on the family dynamics and middle-rade voice. Sasha is doubtful that this trip will be the adventure her parents are promising, while her brother Howard is much more excited for it. But again, this opening isn't doing what it needs to do. If you haven't spotted the pattern between manuscripts one and two yet, this third manuscript will make it all click. This one is adult contemporary romance. I wish I'd left yesterday, but five nights of restless sleep punctuated by bad dreams about the town of Augusta fogged my brain, distracted me from packing. My tour's at 11:00. As long as nothing bad happens on the road today, I'll make it on time. After the second cup of coffee, my heart pound in my fingertips with each step up the three flights to my apartment. I drag the last distended trash bag to the street. The handle of my old cast iron pan pierces the plastic and clanks down the last few steps like a bell at a railroad crossing. At the curb, the mountain of things I've discarded over the last few days narrows the downtown sidewalk, furniture, old medical textbooks, my tragically neglected plants that I hope someone more nurturing will take. Shadow and I scoot around it all. Trained for decisive action, I'm ready to go. But Shadow needs a little encouragement. After a few reassuring rakes through the fur at his neck, he scrambles into the passenger seat. As we pull away, a peach dawn glows on the horizon. The saying goes, "Red sky at dawn. Sailor be warned." Heading to Georgia, a peach sky seems right. An hour and a half later, on the two-lane highway, warm air whips around the interior of the car and over my skin like a frantic caress. Shadow sits at attention, panting in the passenger seat. "You're okay, Shadow." I pet his leg. He's not a head out the window, ears flapping sort. The car stresses him out. His stress mirrors mine. I've got to call my mother or she'll think I'm avoiding her, which I am. Evelyn, I haven't seen you in a while. A pulse blips along my nerves at the sound of my full name. You're about to see a lot more of me. I'm on my way to Augusta for work. This writer has a strong sense of voice, and like in the first manuscript, the narrator immediately expresses some regret and internal conflict. We sense something foreboating awaits her in Augusta, but we don't know what. Overall, we get much less detail on the situation at hand than in the other two manuscripts. But the writer dangles several interesting threads, her old medical textbooks, her upcoming tour, her actively avoiding her mother. And yet, this manuscript has the same problem the other two do. So, what is this mistake that all three novels make? And were you able to spot it? They all open with the protagonist on their way to where the story actually takes place, but nothing of substance is happening to them in the present moment. Manuscript 1 opens with the narrator on a plane descending into Havana. Manuscript 2 opens with a family in a car driving to a seaside town for vacation. And manuscript 3 opens with the narrator cleaning up at her apartment and then driving on the highway toward Augusta, Georgia. In all three cases, we're just watching the protagonist move from point A to point B, and the writer is using that uneventful travel time to provide backstory and exposition. But that's the fundamental problem with this approach. It just gives us setup instead of actually starting the protagonist's journey. Rarely are travel periods exciting in and of themselves. I'm about to get on a plane tomorrow morning and plan to sit there for 4 hours and watch Netflix. So, why would you open your novel with such a boring scene? When you open with a character in transit and they're just reflecting on their life, you're telling the reader, "I know the interesting part hasn't started yet, but just be patient while I catch you up." And I already know what some of you are going to say in the comments. Why are you so impatient? Why can't you just enjoy a few pages of setup? This other novel opens with a character in transit, and it's one of the greatest literary works of all time. Modern literature is terrible because of advice like yours. I get where you're coming from. I really do. But hear me out. I'm not saying you can never have a travel scene. I'm just trying to get you to think seriously about where your story actually begins. Because most writers don't take the time to think about why they're actually leaning on these types of scenes. When I'm editing early drafts of manuscripts, writers almost always start the novel earlier than they actually should. This doesn't only happen with travel scenes, by the way, but those are the most obvious. Another example is when we open with the character waking up, going through their morning routine. Then we see the playbyplay of their entire workday, all before the important action begins. Writers start with these slow scenes because it's typically how the story comes to them. They're trying to ground the reader in who the character is, what their normal life looks like, and what their primary concerns are. All of that is valid and important, but you can still establish who a character is and what they're grappling with in the midst of a charged moment where something consequential is happening. I promise if you do this right, your opening scene is going to be so much more dynamic, propulsive, and engaging. And that's how you pull a reader in from the very first page. So rather than starting your novel with your characters traveling somewhere, try dropping them at their destination on page one. Show them in that new location, facing a hostile welcome or an obstacle they weren't prepared for. You can almost always start your novel later than you think you can, and usually your story will be better for it. There are always exceptions, by the way. And opening with a travel scene does not automatically mean your first pages are bad. But if you're going to do that, something consequential needs to happen during the journey itself that warrants showing it on the page. For example, The Girl on the Train by Paula Hawkins opens with a transit scene done well. We see Rachel's daily commute and the observations she makes during it, but those observations are important because they're the engine of the entire plot. So, it makes sense to open with this. But for my subscribers novels, I think the travel scenes were just being used as background. So, let's talk about how these writers could revise to make for a stronger opening. And it's not as simple as just cutting the travel scene. By the way, if you want to submit your manuscript to me for critique in a future video, make sure to subscribe to my newsletter, Chapter Break, and join the premium tier. You'll receive weekly writing insights from me that I don't post anywhere on this channel, as well as exclusive interviews with literary agents and best-selling authors that are jam-packed with advice for new authors. Let's go back to manuscript one where we see the narrator reflecting on the events that led to her signing up for the Spanish language course in Havana. What if this writer instead opened with the protagonist encountering her very first problem on the ground in Havana? Maybe she can't hail a cab because she can't speak Spanish well enough, which ties back to her need for taking the course. Or maybe she's at the doorstep of her host family and realizes it's the wrong address. or maybe she arrives for her first Spanish lesson and realizes she doesn't have a textbook that everyone else does. That way, we'll see that she's overwhelmed and out of her element without the writer needing to tell us all of this upfront via exposition. And as we're hooked into the action of seeing the narrator navigate this problem, the writer can weave in the background about her secret love and her lateg grandandfather's stories. Now, manuscript 2 is a middle-grade book, but the same principle applies. Right now, the entire opening scene is essentially logistical exposition delivered via dialogue. The parents are explaining what the vacation will be. Sasha is expressing her doubts that it'll be any fun, and her brother Howard is expressing his excitement for it. My suggestion would be to skip the car ride entirely and open with the family arriving at the seaside town. Again, present that first problem they face on their vacation. Maybe the inn the parents booked isn't as it was advertised and that causes a fight between them. Or maybe the fish and chip shop that their dad wanted to go to is boarded up. That way, the adventure will truly start on page one, and that problem will actually give the writer fodder to showcase the family dynamics even more. How do each of them react to the problem? Finally, manuscript 3 has a strong mysterious atmosphere already, but I still think it would benefit from a later starting point. As written, nothing substantial is happening on the page physically. Evelyn drags trash bags from her apartment to the curb, then gets in the car and drives for an hour and a half. Anytime you have a substantial time jump like that on the first page, it may be a sign that you're taking us through a series of inconsequential scenes that we don't really need. These travel preparations do give us buildup, sure, but they're ultimately hurting the narrative momentum and pace. My suggestion is, you guessed it, to start the novel with her already in Augusta. We know she's going there for work, so what happens on her first day at the job? Or potentially she runs into a local who creeps her out. It seems like she's going to see her mother there, so maybe she could be brought into the first scene. That way, we'll get to see and experience all of the dread Evelyn is feeling about Augusta rather than just being told about it in theoretical terms. Figuring out where to open your novel is one of the hardest but most important decisions you'll make as a writer. If you want a professional developmental editor to help you figure out where your story actually starts, submit an inquiry through my website. I've built a team of best-in-class editors who have worked at the world's largest publishing houses and top literary agencies, and we'd love to help you strengthen your story. Opening with a character on the way somewhere is almost always a sign that you're waiting into your story gently instead of jumping right into it. So, I challenge you to look at your own first page and ask yourself honestly, is something consequential happening here, or is my character mostly just thinking and reflecting? If it's the second, open at a later point when the action really gets going and trust that your reader will catch up. Here's a risk-free way to try out a new opening strategy. Open a brand new blank document. Don't touch your original manuscript yet. Then, in the new file, write the scene where your character encounters their first real problem. Write it cold without rereading your old manuscript first. I bet you'll find that you're able to dive right into the heart of the story with ease. You may even find it's easier to weave in the expository and backstory details that the reader needs, and they likely need less setup material than you think they do. So, now that you know where to start your novel, you need to make sure you're not making the other major mistake I see in first pages.   4. @shoemakerspace [1 likes]: Deborah Chester (among others) talks of Scene and Sequel as structural elements; and these words have specific meanings different from common usage.

Scene is something actively changing, usually but not always something external. Action, conflict, challenge.

Sequel follows Scene (usually), and is where the character processes the results of Scene. It’s more internal. The character’s attitude, understanding, or plan changes as a consequence of Scene.

Usually the structure is simple: Scene-Sequel-Scene-Sequel-Scene-Sequel… But sometimes in fast-paced action, you may have Scene-Scene-Scene… as changes come to fast to process. Eventually you have multiple Sequels, or perhaps one large Sequel that reflects on multiple Scenes.

It sounds like the openings you describe jump straight to Sequel without a Scene. The characters reflect before anything has changed. Essentially they reflect on the past which we didn’t see.

I didn't particularly care for any of these openings, but I honestly don't think it had anything to do with where they start the story, because a story is never, no matter the story, about just one location and nothing else. Even in a film like Iron Lung, a story where there is only one location for the entire film, it's not about only that one location, it's about the protagonist's history, his flaws, why he's in the iron lung, who or even what the people talking to him are, and what's down in the blood ocean with him.

The same goes for these stories, where a story takes place is by definition where the story starts, even if the major plot-points have yet to begin.

As I said, I didn't care much for any of these three opening pages, but not for the place the page starts the story at. I just don't care much for everything to be exposited to me by inner-monologue, it feels easy, it feels lazy, it feels like it lacks nuance and the confidence to tell the audience something with an action or a scene. I'm not one of those "show don't tell" cultists who thinks that any diversion from showing is automatically bad exposition, but I'm equally not one fond of what these pages and the millions of stories like them effectively are, which is "tell don't show", the exact opposite extreme.

Now, clearly most people are fine with that, otherwise stories like these wouldn't be all the rage and as much if a monetary monolith as they are in the traditional publishing industry...but that is for me the reason these pages don't work well.

Now, this style of POV can be done well, very well, I don't intend to argue that the style is impossible to write well, just that, like most of not all styles, it too has an inherent flaw; writing in first person, and even third person, with an emphasis on getting inside the character's head, always makes it really easy to tell more than show, and tell more than you should. Which is why I wish writers didn't automatically gravitate towards this style of POV by default.

Richard Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

He's one of the best novelists alive today. This interview is a detailed look at his writing process, inspired by the class he used to teach at Stanford — and he's never done an interview quite like this.

Here are 17 lessons:

1. When you're sure what you're looking at, look harder.

2. There are ultimately only three kinds of novels: (1) Person vs. person, (2) person vs. society, and (3) person vs. environment. 

3. Person vs. Person: This is the psychological novel.

4. Person vs. Society: This is the sociological novel.

5. Person vs. Environment: This type of novel has gone out of style, and Richard is bringing it back. 

6. Clear out the clutter in your life so you can focus on your writing. The fewer complications you have, the more rich and textured your creative process can become. 

7. The best writing advice he's ever received? “Keep your petri dishes open.” Don't tie down your plans or outlines too tightly. 

8. There are two kinds of writers: Top-Down and Bottom Up. 

9. Top-Down writers: Start with the theme and the formal shape that'll drive the story.

10. Bottom-Up writers: Start with people, faces, voices, and local events… then gravitate toward the design of the book.

11. How do you create compelling characters? Push them to the wall. Make them choose between their top two core values. 

12. English speakers are innately bilingual because they can use Latin-inspired words and Anglo-Saxon ones.

13. Editing is the art of excavating what your subconscious mind already knows.

14. When writing dialogue, read it out loud to yourself. That's how readers will read it, too. They'll subvocalize. 

15. For years, Richard wrote and wrote and wouldn't leave the computer until he had 1,000 words on the page. 

16. “If you would learn the secrets of nature, you must practice more humanity.”

17. “The best arguments in the world won’t change a single person’s mind. The only thing that can do that is a good story.”

And finally, what's his goal as a writer? Here it is: “We have this sense that structure is inimical to emotion or that systems are inimical to individuals, that a book can either be a heart book or a head book. And my desire is to write something that's like us, namely an all-in-one.”

- The science of music: Why your brain gets hooked on hit songs | Derek Thompson | Big Think: Kind: captions Language: en One of the questions that I set out to answer in the book is, why do we like what we like in music? What makes music catchy? Where do “earworms” come from? And to answer this really complex question I started with the simplest possible question, which is: what is music? Why does the brain process some sounds as cacophony and other sounds very clearly as song? And to start to answer this question you have to go to Diana Deutsch. And she is a musicologist at the University of California San Diego. And Diana was listening to herself talk at her house one evening, and she put a sentence of hers on repeat and she realized if you take a bit of speech stream and you take a sliver of it and you start repeating it again, start repeating it again, start repeating it again, start repeating it again, start repeat –obviously you can sort of hear it if you’re listening that the brain suddenly starts to hear a melody in this repetition, and a rhythm and a beat, and it starts to hear that which was formally just speech as song. And so what she would say, what I would say, is that repetition is the God-particle of music, it is the thing that distinguishes the cacophony of the world from that which we cannot help but recognize as music. So that’s interesting, but it’s not an answer to the fundamental question, which is: what makes music catchy? Because if I go into a music studio and I say, “start repeating it again, start repeating it again” I’ll be laughed out of the studio immediately. So there has to be a repetition and variety. What is the scientific way to think about the balance? And to answer that question you have to fly northeast from San Diego to Ohio State University in Columbus Ohio, where David Huron did this famous study involving mice where he played a note for a mouse, let’s call it a B note. And the mouse would turn its head like this. And he would play B again, and the mouse would turn its head. And he would play B-B-B and the mouse’s head is just doing this thing. And eventually the mouse habituates, it learns to ignore the stimulus. And habituation is common in culture and life. We learn to ignore things that are too familiar. But if instead at the very moment the mouse is about to habituate from the B note he instead plays a C note, the mouse attends to the C note and is dishabituated from the B note. So now he can go back to scaring the mouse with the B note. And it turns out that if you want to scare a mouse for the longest period of time with the fewest number of notes there’s a very specific pattern that you play, and it goes: B-B-C-B-C-D note to habituate from both from the B and the C note. And as I was reading this study and talking to David I thought, well if you take the letter “B” and you replace it with the word “verse” and you take the letter “C” and you replace it with the word “chorus “and you take the letter “D” and you replace it with the word “bridge,” you have the following song structure: verse-verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge, which is essentially the most common pop song structure of the 20th century. So what seemed so fundamentally interesting to me about this idea is that this same formulaic relationship between repetition and variety that can scare a mouse in a laboratory setting also makes us attend to Top 40 radio in cars. But throughout the book I’m constantly thinking about what are the most important implications of each of these ideas, not only for entertainment, which is interesting but maybe not important, but also for something like politics? And it’s interesting when thinking about repetition and speech and persuasiveness, and realizing that every great rhetorical device is essentially a form of repetition. There is anaphora, which is repetition at the beginning of a sentence. Winston Churchill, “We shall fight them in the landing fields, we shall fight them on the air.” You have tricolon, which is repetition in triplicate. Abraham Lincoln, “Government of the people, by the people, for the people.” There is a lilt to repetition in human speech. But most impressively and maybe most utilized is this thing called antimetabole. And that’s impossible to remember or spell or pronounce so think of antimetabole as A-B-B-A, “Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.” A-B-B-A. “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight, it’s the size of the fight in the dog.” Or Hillary Clinton, “Human rights are women’s rights and women’s rights are human rights,” A-B-B-A, antimetabole. And what I think is so interesting about antimetabole is that it is the most used rhetorical device I think, because it is just musical enough to disguise the fact that it is essentially song, that it is essentially turning human speech into that which the brain wants to process as fluent music. And so sometimes we hear both great ideas and terrible ideas as antimetabole and the brain wants them to be true, and so we like them before we even know to think about them.

- The Anatomy Of A Song: Kind: captions Language: en hey, welcome to 12tone! if you've ever listened to music, you're probably familiar with things like verses and choruses. if you've studied songwriting, you've may have even learned formulas for them. for instance, lots of songs go verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus, done, and that works great, but as a theorist, it's not good enough. what is a verse? what's a chorus? why do they work, and what roles do they play? the answers vary from style to style, and even from song to song, but there's some commonalities we can look at to help us understand why these ideas are, well, everywhere. let's start with the chorus. depending on structure and style, this could also be called a refrain or a hook, and those names kind of give you a clue about what a chorus is. it's a repeated section that's usually the catchiest, most memorable part of the song. but definitions are easy. the interesting question is why. what's the point of repeating ourselves? well, it all comes down to memorability. the chorus is unique but familiar, and it sticks deep in the listener's head. it gives the song its identity. it's the part that everyone can sing along to, and that every fan knows by heart. this is obviously great for marketing, since it creates a sort of musical fingerprint, but it's actually really valuable from an artistic standpoint too. the chorus is like a quick sketch of the entire song. it often tells a short, abstract version of the story, hitting broad, emotional points instead of concrete narrative details. it's more about how you feel, and a good chorus usually serves as a sort of emotional apex, providing context for the rest of the song. typically, because the story is simpler here, the music gets bigger to compensate. ranges broaden, new instruments and voices come in, the melody gets more acrobatic, and everyone gets louder. in fact, the name "chorus" comes from the background singers that tend to join in for this section. all of this helps build that sense of memorability too, because the chorus is where the most interesting things tend to happen. in contrast, verses are often fairly straightforward. that's because they have a different role: they tell the actual story. verses fill in the details that the chorus hinted at. they're much more involved lyrically, so they tend to back off musically to avoid overwhelming the listener. this usually means more restrained melodies and quieter, simpler accompaniment, letting the faster, more complicated lyrics take the spotlight. but that's not to say you can't do anything interesting in a verse: they're a great place for background lines and complex harmonies, since the untrained ear isn't likely to be all that distracted by them. you just have to make sure that the things you add stay in in the background, because the verse is not their time to shine. another common mistake with verses is to write the first one, then just copy and paste the music for all the rest of them, changing only the lyrics from verse to verse. this is tempting, because we just said the background parts don't matter, but, well, you still some variety. the chorus probably isn't changing much, so if the verse isn't either then I've heard everything your song has to offer in the first minute or so, and the rest of it's gonna be repetitive and boring. a good arranger will often add variation between verses, either by changing the melody slightly or by adding new instruments or background lines to help the song build. it's tricky, because you don't want to overwhelm the narrative, but you've got to have some forward motion. and once you've run out of ways to make your verses different, there's one last trick up a songwriter's sleeve: the bridge. this is a section that's completely different, both musically and lyrically, from the rest of the song. it helps break up the monotony of repeated verses and choruses, injecting some new life just as the listener starts to get bored. there are lots of different kinds of bridges, but they tend to have two functions: first, they introduce new musical ideas. this can mean new melodies, new chords, new instruments, or even a new key: remember, at this point your audience is kinda sick of your verse and chorus, so the less like those it sounds, the better. bridges also usually recontextualize the story. this is a bit harder to define, but bridges tend to take a slightly different perspective on events. they give you another way of looking at it. maybe it provides some missing information that helps you see things differently, or maybe it jumps forward in time to a point where the wounds aren't so fresh. or maybe it's something else entirely: narratives are endlessly complex, and there's no shortage of ways to tell them. but if you're just writing it like an extra verse, you're probably wasting an opportunity. of course, those are only a few of the types of sections that can make up a song. we haven't covered intros, breakdowns, solos, prechoruses, or interludes, to name a few. but when it comes to storytelling these are some of the most important ones, and besides, we had to leave something to make another video about. until then, thanks for watching! if you want to help make these videos possible, please consider supporting 12tone on Patreon. you can also join our mailing list for scans of all our episodes, like, share, comment, subscribe, and keep on rockin'.

Through Time song structure consists of different parts that are normally named things like verse Horus Bridge Etc these sections of the song make it easier for The Listener to understand what they're
